### The Masterpiece of the Philosophers

Pour the living gold <note>original: "auri vivi," likely referring to "philosophical" mercury or gold in a liquid state</note> over the red lime <term>red lime: a metallic oxide powder, often produced through calcination</term>, and they will immediately be joined together in an inseparable union. Then, place this mixture into a small glass vessel shaped like a crucible, and ensure it is well-sealed with its lid. Afterward, the vessel should be placed in the lower chamber of the furnace, standing upon a small, well-fired earthen tripod, so that it receives heat from all sides from the upper fire in the second chamber of the furnace. Let it remain there for four natural days.

On the fourth day, take it out. You will find it has become like a bloodstone <note>original: "lapidem sanguineum"</note>, the color of blood—it is, in fact, like blood that has been burnt. Because of the fermentation, add another moderate amount of the aforementioned spiritual and living gold <note>original: "auri spiritualis & vivi"</note> onto it. The powder will very quickly drink up all its moisture and become a moist powder. Cook this powder just as you did before in the second chamber of the furnace with heat surrounding it, and it will become a most deep red color. Oh, what miraculous virtues...

<meta>catchword: ...virtues (virtutes)</meta>

<page-num>187</page-num>

### The Purest Revelation

...virtues are found in this preparation for restoring human health! For it drives away every sickness of whatever condition from human flesh; it preserves the body in its vitality and protects it from all corruption. Indeed, in the common way of speaking about this, life is prolonged through three ages by the movement of the heat emanating or flowing into it, drawing its likeness from its permanent fifth essence <term>fifth essence: also known as the "quintessence," the purest and most medicinal part of a substance, thought to be the celestial element</term>.

Therefore, for human health, take a quantity of this elixir the size of a single grain of wheat. Place it in a large glass jar half-filled with distilled spring water, and heat it over warm ashes. This will most certainly dissolve into a **golden water** <note>original: "aqua aurea"</note> shimmering with intense light. Keep this water in the heat of the sun for as long as the sun is at its height, and keep the vial well-sealed. Know that within nine days, this water changes from tastelessness to a pure and very delightful sweetness for human nature, because of the "digestion" the substance of the water has received from the heat of the medicine, which is now mixed and spread throughout its entire substance.

Of this water, take the amount of one silver spoonful, in whatever way you...

<meta>catchword: ...desire (likely referring to the method of consumption)</meta>

<header>The Mastery of the Philosophers</header>
...whether by itself or mixed with food or drink, or other nourishing liquids, give it to those suffering from illnesses and they shall be healed, whatever the nature of those diseases may be. And this is the **true potable gold** <note>original: *aurum potabile*; a legendary alchemical medicine consisting of gold dissolved or suspended in a liquid, believed to be a universal cure</note>, the water of gold, the moist powder, the marvelous salt that performs wonders and unspeakable things in human bodies; for it works miraculously against **mania** <note>madness or frenzy</note>, **epilepsy**, **apoplexy** <note>strokes or sudden loss of consciousness</note>, **heartburn** <note>original: *cardialgiam*; pain in the heart or upper stomach</note>, **the itch** <note>original: *ploram*; likely referring to scabies or similar skin eruptions</note>, and **leprosy**. It kills every poison and cleanses all that is corrupt; it preserves youth and delays old age; it restores whatever is diminished and consumes whatever is superfluous. It most perfectly cures gouty catarrhs, arthritis, sciatica, and **gout of the feet** <note>original: *podagricos*</note>. It purges and cleanses **black and yellow bile** <note>two of the four "humors" or bodily fluids believed to govern health in pre-modern medicine</note> and phlegm. It creates a good scent in the mouth and in the whole body imperceptibly; it wonderfully strengthens the mind and senses, and sharpens the intellect and reason. It marvelously guards and clears the sight and the power of vision; it cleanses every infection and consumes every poison in the air. It is wonderfully effective during an **epidemic** <note>original: *epidemiam*; often referring specifically to the plague</note>, strengthens the stomach, cures pains of the belly, and settles the **hepatic** <note>liver-related</note> and watery flux. It multiplies natural

<meta>catchword: D</meta>
heat and preserves the **radical moisture** <note>original: *humiditatem radicalem*; the "vital oil" or internal fluid believed to sustain the flame of life</note>, and performs many other acts for the renewal of human nature.

But so that we may use this medicine in another way to heal human bodies: take a quantity of this powder equal to half a grain of wheat in half a glass or more of pure, fresh cow’s milk, and the milk will become a very bright yellow. Give this to **lepers** <note>those suffering from leprosy</note> and the leprosy will most certainly be suppressed and totally annihilated, and the patient shall be healed. Indeed, eventually the skin will wrinkle and be renewed, which is a perfect sign of health. 

However, for the elderly and those who suffer from diseases caused by **cold** <note>in humoral medicine, diseases were categorized as "hot," "cold," "moist," or "dry"</note>, give it with a good, subtle, and fragrant wine. For those who suffer from a **hot** cause, give it with warm water. But for those who are very weak and in need of strengthening, administer it with a good **meat juice** <note>original: *succu carneo*; a restorative broth</note. 

The **careful physician** <note>original: *Medicus circumspectus*</note> should take care that this powder is administered with the liquids closest to human nature: because the more it strengthens nature, the better it will receive the good operation of the medicine. Let him also take heed of what the flavor and substance of a medicine of such great weight ought to be. *D*

It provides specific instructions for a physician to administer the powder using different "carriers"—such as milk, wine, or broth—depending on the patient's age and the elemental nature of their illness.</summary>

# TREATISES
### Contained in this Volume.

I. **The Most True and Most Pure Revelation** *of the* **Most Precious Secret of Secrets, and the Mastery of the Philosophers.** <note>The "Secret of Secrets" (Arcanum Arcanorum) is a common title in medieval and Renaissance occult literature, referring to the ultimate knowledge of nature's hidden powers.</note>

II. **Philosophical Work** *which is called the* **Work of Jupiter**. <note>original: *Opus Jovis*; in alchemical symbolism, Jupiter is the name for the metal tin.</note>

III. **Seven Words of the Philosophers**.

IV. **Two Letters of Antonio de Abatia and Annotations** *on his two* **Letters**. <note>Antonio de Abatia was a 14th-century Italian alchemist whose works were highly regarded for their practical chemical instructions.</note>

V. **Secrets** *derived from a certain* **Anonymous Philosopher**.

-># The Masterpiece of the Philosophers<-
<note>original: "Philosophorum Magisteriū"</note>

The masterpiece is perfected for both the white and the red <note>The "white" (albedo) and "red" (rubedo) are the two final stages of the alchemical work, producing silver and gold respectively.</note> more quickly, promptly, and briefly than other metals that are less "cooked" and "digested." This occurs if the Art, using a very strong agent—the male, that is—arranges it so that the natural powers of digestion prevail within the matter. For the more passive the matter is, and the closer its affinity, the faster it receives the impression from its agent and the sooner it is converted.

Albert <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a scholar and friar often cited as an authority in alchemical texts.</note> says in his book *On Minerals* that it should not escape our notice that in all metallic bodies which undergo "circular generations" <note>The alchemical theory that metals exist in a cycle and can be transformed back and one into another.</note> from one another, the transmutation of those that share more common traits is easier.

Hence, in the science of *Generation* <note>original: "Perigen," likely a reference to Aristotle’s *Peri Geneseos kai Phthoras* (On Generation and Corruption).</note> it is specifically stated that those things which have a greater affinity to each other in their matter, their "digestive" powers, and other natural potencies, are more easily transmuted into one another—*such as Gold and Silver, so that either of them may be transmuted into the other.* <note>original: "Sol, & Luna," the Sun and the Moon, the standard alchemical symbols for Gold and Silver.</note>

Since, therefore, we know that Gold and Silver are of a close "complexion" <note>In medieval science, "complexion" refers to the specific balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>—just like the relationship between male and female—for the purpose of generating the Philosophers' Stone, it is from them that the stone shall be...

<page-num>197</page-num>

->## The Purest Revelation<-
<note>original: "Purissima Revelatio"</note>

...generated. Furthermore, that Silver <note>original: "Lunam"</note> possesses a temperament close to Gold <note>original: "Solem"</note> is made clear by Geber <note>original: "Gebetum"; Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the foundational figure of Islamic alchemy.</note> who says in his *Summa* regarding the examination of metals: "Since Silver does not differ from the nature of Gold by much, with only a small amount of administration, it remains stable alongside Gold in the judgment <note>The "judgment" refers to the test of the furnace or cupellation, where base metals are burned away.</note>, possessing a temperament very close to it."

Likewise, Rhazes <note>original: "Rafis"; Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi, a famous Persian physician and alchemist.</note> says that Silver, among other bodies that fall short of perfection, comes closer to the composition of gold in the balance of its constituent qualities than any other metal. Because it is so near to gold, even though it does not quite reach its standard, it can be healed and purified by a simple artifice and a small "medicine" <note>In alchemy, the "medicine" is another term for the Elixir or the Stone which "cures" imperfect metals into gold.</note>. By this means, the health of the silver is restored through the fixed tincture <note>A "tincture" is the substance that imparts color and permanent quality to a metal.</note> alone.

Similarly, *Ortholanus* <note>A 14th-century alchemist known for his commentaries on the *Emerald Tablet*.</note> says that these two bodies must necessarily be joined together to generate the white and the red stone simultaneously and successively. This is because Silver possesses more temperate and perfect qualities, and is closer to Gold in its "fixation" <note>The ability of a substance to remain stable and not evaporate when exposed to high heat.</note>, its stable temperament, and its degree of "cooking" than any...

<sig>I 3</sig>

Citing authorities like Albertus Magnus, Geber, and Rhazes, the text explains that Silver is an "almost perfect" metal that requires only slight adjustment to become Gold.</summary>

than other metals, and even more than <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum vivum," the metal mercury</note>.

For just as it is necessary for a white body to be transmuted into a red one through a <term>decoction</term> <note>A process of "cooking" or heating a substance in a fluid to extract its essence or change its state.</note> which is above silver by means of the red, so it is necessary first for a red body to be transmuted into a white one by a certain <term>reincrudation</term> <note>A process of returning a "fixed" or mature substance to a "raw" or "crude" state so it can be reworked.</note>, which is below gold by means of the white. And this is because it is necessary that the white stone agree materially with the nature of gold, so that it might more readily receive its <term>tincture</term> <note>The transformative "dye" or soul of the metal that allows it to change other substances.</note> in a closer affinity. This is impossible unless they are joined together, and so that we may have a matter ready for liquefaction; for our final secret is to possess a medicine that melts before the flight <note>evaporation or sublimation</note> of the quicksilver. This is impossible to achieve in such a very short time without the joining together of the Sun and the Moon <note>The alchemical terms for Gold and Silver.</note>.

<term>Hermes</term> <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of the alchemical tradition.</note> says that no paste, whether it be for the white or for the red, can be fermented without gold, and that gold is the ferment for both the white and the red. He also says that the <term>ferment</term> <note>In alchemy, a substance (often gold) added to "leaven" or trigger the transformation of the entire mass, much like yeast in bread.</note> whitens the preparation, prevents it from burning, holds the tincture so that it does not flee, gives life to the physical body, and makes them enter into one

another and be joined, which is the end of the works. By its knowledge, bodies are improved and their work, with the Lord's help, is completed. It is the ferment of the mass, the curdling of the milk, and the musk among spices.

Likewise, <term>Morienus</term> <note>A famous 7th-century hermit and alchemist, teacher to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says that bodies are never perfected until the Sun and Moon, joined into one body, are cast upon them. Therefore, they must be joined together to generate the great <term>Stone of the Philosophers</term>.

<term>Albuhaly</term> <note>Likely referring to an Arabic alchemical authority, possibly Al-Khayyat or a corruption of another name.</note> says that our Philosophy is close to the Sun and the Moon; for although in the generation of the Stone, gold and silver agree in the type of their temperament, they differ in the measures of their qualities. For gold is hotter than silver, while silver is more humid than gold.

If indeed the Sun, as the male, were alone with the volatile quicksilver by itself during generation, the generation would be hindered by the insufficiency of the passive matter close to it. This matter could in no way be contained in the quicksilver alone because of the too great distance between the two of them, and the great separation of the primary qualities which

<meta>This page continues a discussion on the alchemical generation of the Philosopher's Stone, specifically focusing on the relationship between mercury, gold, and silver. The previous sections likely established the elemental qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) required for transmutation.</meta>

<page-num>100</page-num>

# ->The Masterpiece of the Philosophers<-

[They] are in **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento vivo"; mercury</note> much contrary to the temperament of **gold**: nor even in gold itself due to the insufficiency of another **passive matter** closer to it in those contrary qualities which are required for a nearby generation. And therefore [it must seek] another sex that is closer in the temperament of heat and cold; for it was necessary that the **lunar body** <note>original: "corpus lunare"; refers to silver</note> whose **lime** <term>calx: the powdery substance left after a metal is heated or "calcined"</term> with its **menstrual blood** <note>original: "sanguine menstruali"; an alchemical term for the solvent or transformative fluid that "nourishes" the growing Stone</note>, in white **quicksilver**, or as the first passive and receptive matter, should be in the aforementioned generation, and that in that matter there should be two qualities fit for the receptacle of the **tinctures** <note>original: "tincturarum"; the transformative colors or essences in alchemy</note>, namely the **cold**—not excessive, but temperamental—and the **material moist**; and this is **silver** reduced to its first matter.

But since the passive matter is also not formative in generating the **stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note>, it is necessary to have artificial instruments suited to active formation; and these are the **well-moving heat** and **well-penetrating dryness**. And when these two active qualities prevail in something, then the cold cannot overcome the well-moving heat of the forms, since it is not superior to it but merely temperamental, and the moist is well-receiving since it is proportionate to it...

<meta>catchword: proportionate</meta>

We have clearly demonstrated the operation; now it remains to discuss the **matter of the stone** <term>Matter of the stone: The primary raw material (materia prima) used to create the Philosopher's Stone.</term>.

We have said that the matter of metals is **quicksilver** <term>Quicksilver: Latin *argentum vivum*, the liquid metal mercury.</term> and **sulfur**, which are cooked together by mineral heat and turned into either a perfect or an imperfect metal. And in truth, the matter of the stone is nothing other than sulfur and quicksilver cooked, and afterwards purified by art.

However, this must not be understood as common, raw, impure, and imperfect quicksilver, because that cannot be the matter of the stone.

**The first reason:** Anything impure and imperfect can in no way perfect or purify another thing. Common mercury is such a substance; therefore, it cannot purify or perfect other metals, but rather infects them when it is mixed with them.

**The second reason:** That which perfects metals must itself possess perfection; and the perfection of all things consists in an equal conjunction of purified **elements** <term>Elements: In alchemy, these are Earth, Air, Fire, and Water, which must be balanced to achieve stability.</term>. The "mediums" between them are more cooked and more purified, approaching the form of gold or silver, but such matter is not common raw quicksilver.

### Concerning the division and order of Philosophical 
### sublimation, and the required 
### operations.

Just as the body is divided by its members, and all members are reduced to one composite whole, which is the body: so our Philosophical sublimation is divided into separate parts, yet all tend toward one final perfect disposition. The Philosophers have said that the first part of this sublimation is the **dissolution of the Body** <note>The initial breaking down of the "body" or metallic source into a liquid form.</note>.

The second part they have named **putrefaction** <note>A stage of decay or "blackening" (nigredo) where the substance is broken down by gentle heat.</note>.

The 3rd is sublimation, or the separation of water from earth.

The 4th is the **calcination** <term>Calcination: Heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or "ash," representing the death of the old form.</term> of the body separated from water.

The 5th is the distillation of the waters.

The 6th is **imbibition** <note>Literally "drinking"; the process of adding liquid back to the dried matter.</note> or feeding, and the mortification of the species.

The 7th is the **resurrection of the dead** <note>A symbolic term for the stage where the substance begins to regain "life" or volatile properties after being reduced to ash.</note>.

The 8th is the washing and **resolution** <note>The final breaking down or softening of the purified matter.</note> of the calcined body.

### On the Cause of the Variation of the Names of this Sublimation.

Therefore, I say that this work of **sublimation** <term>Sublimation: The process of heating a substance to turn it into vapor and then back into a solid; alchemists saw this as a way to "spiritualize" heavy matter.</term> is the first rectification of the **Stone** <term>The Philosophers' Stone: The ultimate goal of alchemy, a perfected substance representing the union of spirit and matter.</term>, or the preparation of **mercury** <term>Mercury: For the alchemist, "mercury" was the volatile, living spirit within all matter, not just the liquid metal we know today.</term>, a process unknown to many modern practitioners. They fall into error because of the variety of names used by the Philosophers to describe it.

For some of them call this sublimation "dissolution," some "washing," some "distillation," and others "calcination." The reason for their intention, which moved them to use these different names, is this: the substance that is sublimated is liquefied by the heat before it flies up from the fire. Since everything that can be melted is of the nature of water—as has been proven by *Albert* <note>original: *Alberto*; refers to Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar whose works on minerals were foundational to later alchemy.</note> in his book on minerals—they have called this work of sublimation a **dissolution**

into mercury, regarding the final goal of the operation.

By a third reason, it is called **dissolution** because the bond created by nature—namely, the union of the combustible and earthy parts of the silver with the subtle parts—is broken and dissolved by the fire. This allows the most pure, subtle parts to be raised up, leaving behind the thick, corrupting elements. *Mirendus* <note>original: *Mirendus*; likely a reference to an alchemical authority, possibly a corrupted name for Pico della Mirandola or a similar figure citing the spiritualization of matter.</note> testifies to this, saying: "It is necessary for the body to be liquefied, so that its bodily nature may be altered, until the body is destroyed by dissolution and becomes spiritual and thin, etc."

### Concerning the Corruption and Putrefaction of Dissolved Things.

Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it brings forth much fruit. <note>A quote from the Gospel of John 12:24, frequently used by alchemists to explain that a substance must be "destroyed" or "killed" to be reborn as something more perfect.</note> Similarly, in the philosophers' stone, unless the gold or silver converted into mercury dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it brings forth much fruit. 

The philosophers, introducing this authority, said that he who knows how to mortify <note>To "kill" or strip away the outward physical form of a metal.</note> and, after death, to vivify <note>To bring back to life; to reanimate the purified essence.</note>, is the master of this art. In other words, they repeat this again by saying: he who knows how to make the hidden manifest and the manifest hidden <note>This refers to the alchemical goal of making the inner "spirit" visible while making the outer "body" invisible or spiritualized.</note> contains his work within himself and may say that he knows all things. We do all these things, therefore, through mortification and the putrefaction <note>The stage where the material decays and turns black, considered essential for its eventual transformation.</note> of dissolved things, since putrefaction is the mother of all things and the cause of generation, as well as the cause of animation and the separation of heterogeneous <note>Foreign or impure substances that do not belong to the core material.</note> matters; it is also the cause of the unity of the original things.

# The Mastery of the Philosophers
<meta>catchword: ...bound [original: "tur"]</meta>

...of the origins, and the birth of the Elixir <term>Elixir: In this context, the transformative substance or "Philosopher’s Stone" that can transmute base metals or grant long life.</term>.

Therefore, we must consider nothing except the causes of putrefaction <term>Putrefaction: The stage of alchemical "death" or decomposition, where the material turns black and breaks down, allowing its inner "spirit" to be released.</term>. For we see that from putrefaction, worms are generated through the boiling and rotting caused by heat introduced into moisture, in which the nature of the worm consists. Likewise, from the underlying metallic matter, we see the Elixir generated through putrefaction. Indeed, everything pertaining to the perfection of our mastery <note>original: "magisterii," referring to the "Great Work" or the achievement of the alchemical goal.</note> comes from putrefaction; from putrefied things they are born, and from there all strength proceeds. For from a strong mixture of gold or silver, or similar things, substances become fragile, and from fragile things, they become strong.

The cause of the division of the Elements <term>Elements: The four basic building blocks of matter (Earth, Air, Fire, and Water).</term> is therefore putrefaction, which moves and unites raw elements with "cooked" <note>In alchemy, "cooked" refers to substances that have been matured or processed by heat.</note> elements, by way of alteration and not dissipation, and they are mixed together. Then the complexion <note>original: "complexio," the specific balance of qualities—hot, cold, moist, or dry—that defines a substance’s nature.</note> of the metal is corrupted and changed, and the elements begin to move away from one another and are set in motion. And since the bond of their mixture is not strong at that time because of their contrariety, each of the elements then escapes and is separated from the other. Putrefaction is also the cause of a perfect mixture, because through it they are bound—

<column-break/>

# Most Pure Revelation
<meta>catchword: Of [original: "De"]</meta>

—the elements are bound together so that they cannot further be separated from one another. For although putrefaction first corrupts and divides, such a division only concerns the corruptible and corrupting things within the matter, since these are not—nor can they be—part of the proportion of the harmonizing Elements. These elements, once dissolved by putrefaction, nature strives with all her strength to join into one, and to bind together inseparably. 

But because these Elements are foul and impure and out of proportion, this foulness and impurity prevent the contact of the putrefied things that are to be joined through union. Therefore, putrefaction itself cannot inseparably bind the elements together until after their perfect cleansing from every corrupting thing. For this reason, the elements are separated after they have been putrefied, so that they may be more refined and purified of all dregs <note>original: "sordibus," literally filth or dross.</note>, so that they may afterwards be joined into the Elixir through putrefaction. From these things, you may draw out the secret: that the entire Mastery is nothing but putrefaction and mortification <term>Mortification: The "killing" or stripping away of a substance's outward form to reach its inner essence.</term>, so that things may arrive at incorruptibility and immortality, perpetuity, and an indelible life forever.

### On the essential putrefaction and mortification of the stone.

The beginning of putrefaction is moisture, but its true end is dryness and reduction to ash <term>incineration: The process of heating a substance until it is reduced to a dry, fine powder, representing the final stage of a substance's physical "death."</term> and, consequently, the "mortification" or killing of the living moisture.

Therefore, it is necessary to rot and corrupt the radical moistures <term>radical moisture: The essential, internal life-fluid believed to reside within all matter; in alchemy, this must be "fixed" or stabilized to create the Stone.</term> which have been brought to life. This is done through their mutual mortification <term>mortification: The alchemical process of "killing" a substance by stripping away its outward characteristics to reach its inner essence.</term>, according to the way the qualities of the "mortifying" Element overcome the qualities of the "living" Element—which is a great secret.

Indeed, the mortifying Elements are earth and water, with a specific distinction between two types of mortification. The first occurs when the animated water <note>original: "aqua animata," referring to water that contains the "air" or spirit/life-force.</note>—in which air resides—is converted into a dead earthy substance, or a dead powder. This happens because the qualities of the earth predominate and enter into its substance; and because this is the action of the earth, the water so animated is converted into the likeness of earth. The earth assimilates the water to itself, although the color must necessarily change, as a result of the variation—

---

# Purissima Revelatio.
<note>original: "The Purest Revelation"</note>
<sig>D</sig>
<meta>catchword: deter</meta>

—of variation and foulness. For this reason, if the water were pure and of a white nature, it would be mortified into a white powder, just as its earth is, if that earth be white; likewise, if the water were pure and of a red nature, it would be mortified into a true redness—which is also a great secret.

The other mortification occurs when the earth—in which there is a living and moving fire, which is the hidden fire <term>hidden fire: An internal, chemical heat or "spirit" within matter, distinct from the physical flame of a furnace.</term>—is converted along with water into the substance of a congealed stone. This happens because the qualities of the water then predominate, entering and surrounding its substance. And because water performs this operation, the earth so composed of elements is turned into the likeness of "earthy water"—that is, into a congealed mass <note>original: "coagulum."</note> having within itself a metallic appearance <note>original: "speciem metallicam."</note> derived from the nature of the water. This is because the water, through a proportional mixture, acted more effectively as an instrument against the earth than the earth did against the water; therefore, the earth received more of the appearance of "living water" than the water received of the appearance of "deadly earth."

For you should know that many secrets lie hidden under the proportions of this kind of mortification in nature, and through it, the principles of this art are known—namely, of the [determined] matter... <meta>The catchword "deter" suggests the next page begins with "determinatæ" (determined or specific).</meta>

The measure of internal things is nature itself. For **generosity** <note>original: "liberalitas." The author uses the moral virtue of generosity as an analogy for the chemical process: just as being generous is about the right intent rather than just the amount of money given, alchemical "feeding" is about the right proportion rather than the volume of liquid.</note> does not consist in a multitude of waters, but in the habit of virtue through the faculty of the converting power. Therefore it is said: use neither much nor little, but a moderate natural weight of the **glorified water** <term>glorified water: An alchemical term for a purified, distilled, or spiritually "rectified" liquid solvent used to process the stone.</term> which God has deigned to bestow upon you, so that you do not pour it in beyond measure, lest you fall into the vice of extravagance, nor cut it back too far, but always hold the middle path in all things. 

Namely, you should not pour in a multitude of water except according to the service and power of the converting virtue; and thus the virtue itself will be multiplied, both in quality and substance, in both Elements—that is, in earth and in water. # The Mastery of the Philosophers
<page-num>84</page-num>
<header>The Mastery of the Philosophers</header>
<meta>catchword: water (aqua)</meta>

A measured regimen is found in nature: and for this reason, nature looks toward the middle path and works through it. Since nature—the partner with whom **art** <note>original: "ars." In alchemy, "art" refers to the skill and labor of the human chemist working upon natural substances.</note> operates—is proportioned by the ratio of the form we desire, she leads her matter toward its own proportion. Therefore, the Philosophers say that the artisan fares well if he works with nature and through nature: for she, in all her operations, observes the quantities and proportions in the measures of the elements determined for the generation of the **Philosopher’s Stone** and gold. These quantities and proportions of the mixture are known to nature alone. By preparing her own matter and refining it from **corrupting sulfur** <term>corrupting sulfur: In alchemical theory, sulfur was a "father" principle of metals, but "common" or "corrupting" sulfur was believed to cause impurities and prevent the formation of gold.</term>, she hides the forms, saves the natures, guards the proportions, and alters the colors from the beginning to the end.

Furthermore, in nourishing and generating the elements of the stone, soak the earth—as I have said above—with a small amount of water, and let them be mixed together. This means that water must be mixed into the earth, and similarly the earth into the water, and they should always remain in the form of a powder. Let it be soaked further as if by **dew** <note>original: "roraticè." This suggests a very light, mist-like application of liquid rather than pouring.</note>, by pouring the water over the earth.

<column-break/>

<page-num>85</page-num>
<header>Most Pure Revelation.</header>
<meta>catchword: Since (Cùm)</meta>

...with its stated water, so that it remains a powder; and when the earth and the entire matter have been soaked and reduced to powder, soak it again little by little as described above. However, a definite weight for this **soaking** <term>imbibition: (Latin: imbibitio) The process of "feeding" a dry substance with liquid, allowing it to absorb the moisture without becoming a slurry or liquid.</term> cannot be given, because sometimes the power of nature is stronger, and sometimes it is weaker. Instead, the Philosophers recur to the strength of nature, saying: use neither much—because nature would not be able to digest it—nor too little, because the matter would then be scorched, and a **redness** would be generated before the **blackness**, which is a sign of burning. 

For it is necessary first to generate the blackness and to remain in that state for some time before other colors follow from the renewal of the fire or heat. Nevertheless, all colors that appear after the blackness are to be praised. Yet the blackness is not generated suddenly, but successively and gradually, and it will increase from one **decoction** <term>decoction: The process of heating or "boiling" a substance in a closed vessel to refine it.</term> to the next until it reaches its limit, at which point another color succeeds it. The blackness, therefore, demonstrates the measure of the soaking, since the heat then has sufficient material upon which to act; and thus the heat, acting upon the matter, generates the blackness.

### Why the Philosophers have called this stone an "egg": the consequence is to be noted.

The reason why the Philosophers call this stone an **egg** <note>The "Philosophical Egg" is a central alchemical metaphor representing the vessel and the matter within, containing all the potential for new life/perfection.</note> is this: namely, because just as an egg is a round, circular thing, containing within itself two natures in one substance—the **white** <term>white: original "albumen."</term> and the **yolk** <term>yolk: original "vitellum."</term>—and from itself it extracts another thing having a soul, life, and generation, namely that a chick is born from it: so this stone contains within itself two things of one nature, namely the body and the spirit, and it extracts from itself a soul and life. As *Menaldus* says in the *Assembly* <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*; one of the earliest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a meeting of ancient philosophers.</note>: "The thick, earthy part does not dye, but the subtle nature which is in the body is transfigured and gives color." For this reason, the Philosophers said that copper does not dye unless it is first dyed. *Geber* <note>Geber: The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the 8th-century polymath and "father of chemistry."</note>, gifted with marvelous ingenuity, testifies that this work of sublimation must be done, saying in the chapter on medicines of the third order: "Take the known stone, and let the stone be most perfectly cleansed by the method of separation already described." And *Alphidius* <note>Alphidius: A legendary Arab alchemist frequently cited in medieval European manuscripts.</note> says to the king: "Let the fire be between strong and gentle, until the spirit has receded from the body and ascended on high, just as black clouds rise over the earth, and the body will remain at the bottom of the vessel without its spirit." And *Bellus* says in the book of the *Assembly*: "The knowledge of this art is nothing else than..."

### *Concerning the rotation of the stone with the repetition of the second circle.*

To **rotate** the stone by circulating it <note>original: *rotare verò lapidem circulando*; this refers to the "Circulation of the Philosophers," a repetitive cycle of evaporation and condensation intended to spiritualize the matter.</note> is to again return the moist over the dry, by grinding it in turns and gradually soaking it, and by boiling it for four days at a time, and afterwards sublimating the volatile part, then gently calcining the matter remaining at the bottom, and gathering that which was sublimated. Thus, continue this soaking and drying until the water has been totally **mortified**—that is, to repeat the previous operations as has already been said.

### *On the Perfection of the Elixir of the first degree and its composition.*

When, therefore, the **quicksilver** <note>original: *argentum vivum*; the metal mercury, considered by alchemists to be the "mother" of all metals.</note> has been cleansed through the preparations of the first degree and reduced into a most pure and shining substance, two further preparations are required. One of these is **hardness** along with the **glowing** <note>original: *ignitione*; the state of being heated until it glows red, without vaporizing.</note> of its fusion; this is achieved with its **fixed sulfur**, or **fixed arsenic**, which is the **lime** <term>lime: (Latin: *calx*) the powdery metallic ash left over after a substance has been "burned" or oxidized by intense heat.</term> of the "body" with which the quicksilver was prepared. For the fixed quicksilver—that is, the lime of the body—grants the quicksilver the ability to melt while glowing, so that it does not flee from the fire. There will be, therefore, a hardening of its soft substance along with the glowing of its fusion. This means we must find a way to thoroughly mix into the depths of that pure quicksilver the **fixed substance** or lime, which is called "sulfur" and "arsenic." This is because it mixes and unites easily with it, hardening and coagulating it so that the material does not melt before it reaches a glowing heat. We shall reveal this method further below. The other preparation, indeed, is for **fixation**, achieved by removing its

### *On the method of hardening, and of mixing and coagulating quicksilver.*

Take one ounce of the purest **silver** <note>original: *lunæ*; literally "Moon," the alchemical name for silver.</note> purified three times by the **cupel** <term>cupel: (Latin: *copellam*) a small, porous bowl used in a furnace to separate precious metals from lead or other impurities.</term>, so that it is well-cleansed of all superfluous moisture, pure and dry. Dissolve it in our quicksilver that was sublimated above and worked through the first degree. This dissolution is done as we have described in other dissolutions, so that the entire silver is converted into **mercury**, or into a most brilliant quicksilver, and passed through a linen filter. Next, separate the liquid substance from the fixed substance by squeezing it through a tight filter. Grind this fixed substance upon a stone, and let it be **imbibed** <term>imbibing: (Latin: *imbibatur*) the process of slowly adding liquid back into a dry powder to nourish it or change its consistency.</term> bit by bit with its own water that was separated by the filter. However, always keep grinding and imbibing until it becomes a **paste**. Take this paste

# ON THE FINAL INTENTION
## *which the craftsman ought to have.*

SINCE the Human Body has no [finite] value according to any law—because all things **were made for its sake** <note>original: *facta sunt propter ipsum*; a common theological sentiment that the physical world was created to serve humanity.</note>—those philosophizing in this art should desire these medicines more for life and health than for acquiring riches. These medicines, being of the **quintessence** <term>quintessence: the "fifth essence" or purest element, believed to be the life-force of all matter.</term>, are above all other medicines for healing any bodily infirmities whatsoever, regardless of their cause—whether **hot or cold** <note>Referring to the four humors (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile) and their associated qualities.</note>. For riches are left behind in a short time with great sorrow and perhaps even lethally; and since the most excellent treasure which ought to be expected by everyone after the **salvation of the soul** <note>original: *salutem animae*.</note> is health, without which we can enjoy no happiness in this life, I shall explain clearly and without evasion the true secret of the **universal medicine** and reveal the true **potable gold** <term>potable gold: *aurum potabile*, a fabled liquid gold supplement thought to grant eternal youth or perfect health.</term> of the Philosophers.

### Drinkable Gold of the Philosophers in the first degree.

If you wish to prepare gold for the healing of human bodies, take <note>original: *℞* (recipe)</note> one ounce of the purest gold, purified through cementation <note>a dry-refining process using salts and heat to purge gold of impurities.</note>, and dissolve it in our **mercury** prepared through the first degree of sublimation—that is, in our **red water**, already prepared and animated as described above and separated from its body. You should know that this water—namely, our mercury—will entirely devour the gold itself. Concerning this, Socrates, in his *Treatise on the Eagle*, says: *Behold how the viper, his wife, swallows him* <note>original: *Videas qualiter ipsum transglutiat vipera conjux sua*; here the "viper" is the corrosive mercurial solvent and the "husband" is the gold.</note>. He clearly signifies that the dissolution of gold ought to be performed by means of our prepared mercury, specifically that which has been stripped of all venom.

But when it has been dissolved and well-refined, separate all its moisture through **philosophical sublimation** <note>a process of vaporizing and re-condensing a substance to purify it.</note>, and at the bottom of the vessel, the **fixed and dead earth** will remain; dry this. Once the earth is dried, take the water that was separated from it and return it to the earth, joining them together in turn and marrying it to her **red husband** <note>the gold, now in a reactive state</note> until

### *Here follows the second stage, which concerns the greater purification and refinement of the stone itself through the separation of the elements.*

The second stage of the stone consists of taking the matter already prepared through the first stage, and dissolving the calxes <note>original: "calces"—the dry, powdery remains of a substance after it has been roasted or "calcined."</note> separately according to the teaching handed down above, so that the whole becomes like a most shining quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"—literally "living silver," the common name for mercury.</note>. This dissolution is performed no differently than in the other aforementioned dissolutions. Once the matter is dissolved and converted into mercury, purified and refined, and worked with great skill, prepare the fire appropriate for sublimation <note>The process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again in a purer form.</note>. Sublimate all the matter that can be sublimated, increasing the fire by degrees; do not increase the fire suddenly, lest there be a "sea of confusion" <note>original: "pelagus conturbationis"—a poetic way of describing a chaotic chemical reaction where the process is ruined.</note> and a loss of the virtues by the force of the fire.

For you should know that the heat existing in the mineral is sometimes so crushed and weighed down by the coagulation of its own matter that it can in no way move itself toward the perfection of its matter, unless it is assisted

---

<page-num>161</page-num>
<header>The Purest Revelation.</header>
<meta>catchword: because</meta>

by a sharper lance <note>original: "lance"—metaphorically referring to the piercing intensity of the flame.</note>, namely by a stronger fire piercing it from the outside. And sometimes it is sufficient to continue the fire, always maintaining it in a single state until the perfection of the sublimation is reached, without any strengthening of the heat. This is because at that point the internal natural heat is so strong, and multiplied in such quantity within its mineral, that after it has been stirred into motion, the mere continuation of the external fire is sufficient for it until the completion of its sublimation. Because the natural heat, multiplied throughout its entire matter, is diffused, dispersed, and mixed in, it resolves itself everywhere, crushing its fixed matter and converting it into an ashy powder. Likewise, it sometimes brings its moisture to an end through sublimation, turning it into a powder; this signifies that the winning and dominating heat is present in the matter. Sometimes this powder is volatile <note>A substance that easily evaporates or turns into gas.</note>, and sometimes it is not, which happens according to whether the total amount of the volatile overcomes the total amount of the fixed <note>original: "fixi"—the stable part of the substance that resists the fire.</note> in the mixture, or is overcome by the fixed part. And sometimes it is a white powder, and sometimes not (if it came from the white); and sometimes it is red, and sometimes not (if it came from the red), because...

### *What the egg generated from the dead egg may be.*

### *What the thing is that must be separated from a thing elementally according to nature.*

Furthermore, that which is universally warmer throughout the whole substance of the liquid must be separated from the air in the substance of oil or fire. When this has been done, the separation of the elements will be perfected.

### *How the aforementioned elements are known to be present in the composition of the quicksilver of the Philosophers.*

**T**hat this quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"—mercury</note> of the Philosophers contains within itself the four elements is demonstrated by this: since at the time of its mortification <note>In alchemy, "mortification" refers to the symbolic death or chemical breakdown of a substance, often marked by a change in color or state.</note> you saw hardness and dryness in it, which necessarily must be produced from the portion of earth existing within it; you similarly saw an actual redness in it, which must necessarily proceed from the portion of fire existing within it; you also saw, at the time of its resurrection <note>The stage where the "dead" substance is revived or made fluid again.</note>, softness and an actually cold moisture in it, which must naturally arise from the portion of the element of water within it; you also saw in it a viscous and binding moisture from the same, at the time when dry and mortified things are imbibed <note>The process of "imbibition" involves slowly adding liquid to a dry solid until it is saturated.</note>: For the binding power is that which, by its viscosity, causes divided parts to stick together, which are nonetheless legitimately produced from the parts existing in the air <note>The author attributes the cohesive, "sticky" quality of the substance to the element of air.</note>.
<meta>catchword: Through</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>167</page-num>

Through the first [quality, dryness], nature dries and retains itself; through the second [moisture], it softens and dissolves itself; through the third [heat], it digests and divides itself; and through the [fourth] quality, it unites and binds the divided parts together by sticking to one another.

Since, therefore, an assertion of this kind is confirmed by the philosophy of *Rasis* <note>Al-Razi (c. 865–925 AD), a Persian physician and alchemist whose works were fundamental to medieval European science.</note>, namely that (as was alleged above) the heat of fire, the cold of water, the moisture of air, and the dryness of earth joined together contain a perfect and complete element: He is and shall be blind to their separation from each other who finds difficulty in believing these things.

### *Concerning the difficulty and the ingenuity required for the separation of the elements.*

And especially since all the Philosophers say that quicksilver, by no means of destruction <note>original: "exterminationis"—here meaning the total breaking down or driving out of components.</note>, allows itself to be divided or separated into its component parts...

### Response to the foregoing arguments.

**A**nd we, in response, say that those things which are joined together by nature and with nature, are also separated from one another by nature and with nature. This separation occurs without the corruption of the parts, or

<meta>catchword: or</meta>

---

<page-num>169</page-num>
<header>Most Pure Revelation</header>

the destruction of the natural parts that are separable from one another into their elemental components—that is, by elemental composition only. On account of this, the insightful observer says in truth that such a separation is not a "division" <note>In this context, "division" implies breaking something so thoroughly that it loses its identity or "form."</note>, because it would thus be destroyed from its form; rather, it is a mixture, which is the union of altered things capable of being mixed. For just as nature there joins the hot with the cold and the dry with the moist, dissolving them by its digestive <note>original: "digestiva"—in alchemy, a process of slow, gentle heating like biological digestion</note> and purifying <note>original: "mundificativa"</note> power: so this same nature, by resolving them through its other powers—which are called attractive and (he adds) appetitive <note>The "appetitive" power refers to the natural "hunger" or tendency of substances to seek out and join with their like.</note>—separates them into their elemental parts by means of art <note>The "Art" refers to the skill and intervention of the alchemist working alongside nature.</note>. Hence says *Arnaldus de Villanova* <note>Arnaldus de Villanova (c. 1240–1311) was a famous physician and alchemist; his "Medicinal Mirror" is a key medieval text.</note> in his *Medicinal Mirror*: that the operations of these powers cannot be contemplated except by the natural worker <note>The alchemist who follows nature's laws.</note> alone.

It should be noted that the elements are not divided within the stone according to their physical substance, because that same substance is always indissoluble—which is called **mercurial** <note>In alchemy, "mercurial" refers to the fundamental, fluid essence of matter, not necessarily the common metal mercury</note>—but they are separated according to their **virtue** <note>original: "virtutem," meaning their inherent power or active property</note>, so that one virtue may be separated from another, or one quality from another. Throughout this, the substance of any of these qualities always remains under that same mercurial form, since no pure, simple element is found in nature except within its own specific sphere.

## On the Art of Generating a Human Being

Although we stated above that art generates a human being, you should not understand this except as a matter of "disposition" <note>The author distinguishes between creating life from scratch (which only God/Nature can do) and "disposition," which means arranging the necessary conditions for nature to act.</note>. Indeed, no one can artificially produce human seeds <note>original: "spermata"</note> perfectly, but we are certainly able to dispose a human being toward their own productive generation through art. For vital seeds are digested by nature alone in a vegetative way within the loins of both parents, and are drawn out from foods and drinks that have been artificially prepared. Afterward, we mix these through intercourse in natural vessels. Both intercourse and the administration of food and drink are described as the "art" that prepares the dishes for the generation of seeds, and from there, the seeds for the joining that generates a human. For example, in the nature of man, the male seed—as something more mature, more digested, more perfect, and more active—is joined artificially with the female seed, which is less mature, namely the passive seed.

For the first seed <note>the male</note> contains more of the active elements within itself in actuality, such as air and fire; therefore, it is more active in digesting and refining the passive elements. The sec-

For this reason, *Arnaldus* <note>Arnaldus de Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist</note> says in his *Mirror*: "the generating things are indeed the place and the individual of the species." Note, therefore, the material degree, so that the matter is well-disposed according to the degrees of the form it must receive. This is because the more the matter is prepared, the more the form shines within it; and the less it is prepared, the less the form shines. This form is truly from the <term>fifth essence</term> <note>original: "substantia quinta"—the quintessence, a pure, incorruptible state of matter beyond the four earthly elements.</note> which, when it comes to the matter, perfects it and joins with it to achieve its perfection. When this is joined, the **elixir** is composed; and when it is destroyed, nothing of the substance of the elixir remains. This is clearly seen in the works of the sophists <note>original: "sophisticorum"—referring to fraudulent alchemists or those who use "tricks" rather than true natural philosophy.</note>, which are entirely foreign to nature.

Furthermore, form combined with matter is the cause of all "accidents" and all colors. However, an accidental form <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that can change (like color or temperature) without changing the core essence of the thing itself.</note> does not perfect the matter, nor does it preserve it in its being, as is gathered from the 8th book of Aristotle's *Metaphysics*. We must therefore take note of accidental colors which do not remain in the final result. Every actual form requires a substantial form, just as the male requires the female according to the capacity of the matter, which is the cause of the actual form. Because every form is simpler, more active, and more noble than matter, it is concluded (according to Aristotle in the book *On Animals* <note>original: "Arist. lib. de animali"</note>)

But according to the requirements of the nobility of the form that is to be impressed upon the matter, the matter must be disposed and prepared as has been said. Otherwise, the matter would not receive the form because of its own inability.

Through this doctrine, it is demonstrated why <term>mercurius</term> <note>Mercury, often called "Quicksilver" by the alchemists.</note> must first be sublimated, whether in general or in particular—that is, both for the <term>universal medicine</term> and for specific ones. This is what it means to **sublimate**: namely, to prepare the matter by removing it from its opposites until it possesses a likeness of equality to heaven, and is of the nature of the fifth essence, which entirely preserves every living thing from corruption.

### *Doctrine of Weights.*

IN the generation of the Philosopher’s Stone, you must know in what weight the "altering agent" <note>The active, medicinal component of the work.</note> ought to be mixed with the "alterable substance" <note>The base matter being transformed.</note>: because the operation of the composition will be according to the weights of the components—namely, the elements. For in that which one exceeds another, it brings it to perfection; but that in which it is exceeded by the other, it is itself brought to perfection <note>This describes a reciprocal relationship where the stronger element transforms the weaker into a new, perfected state.</note>. Thus, the medicine or stone, according to the measure of its quantity, sometimes tints the mixture, and sometimes is itself tinted by the mixture. For if the medicine is of the correct weight, whatever color it may be, it will color the mixture with its own hue; however, if a small quantity of it is overcome by the mixture, it will be colored by that mixture instead. Hence it is that one and the same medicine serves for both the white and the red work <note>The "White" work (albedo) creates silver, while the "Red" work (rubedo) creates gold.</note>. Since, therefore, "citrinity" <note>original: "citrinitas." A yellowing stage that traditionally occurs between the white and red phases of the process.</note> is nothing other than a specific proportion of white and red, it is certain that if the weights of the aforementioned components—namely, the red and the white—exceed the specified portion, there will no longer be citrinity in its balanced degree,

### On the altering qualities.

It is also necessary for you to have knowledge of the primary qualities <note>The four basic Aristotelian qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> and of those virtues by which they act, alter, and are altered. This is so that through this knowledge, the power of the "alterer" <note>The active agent or catalyst in the chemical reaction.</note> can be better strengthened and multiplied over the power of the "alterable" <note>The base material being changed.</note>, and so that the alterable qualities can be brought closer to the qualities of the alterer. If you know how to do this, you will be able to arrive most perfectly first at the perfect whiteness <note>original: "albedinem perfectam," the second major stage of the Great Work, associated with silver.</note>, and successively at the yellowness <note>original: "citrinitatem," an intermediate stage between white and red.</note>, and finally at the most deep-red color. From all the things mentioned above, it is clear that there are three things we must know: namely, the proportion of the components, their qualities, and the form or method of their mixing.

It should also be noted that sometimes certain medicines are more intense than others in their redness, while others are less so. ### *How the matter which has been made spiritual and pure, and of the nature of heaven, may be made fixed and of the nature of the glorified earth, by receiving both powers, namely the spiritual and the corporal.*

But since the aforementioned *matter of the stone* <term>materia lapidis: the base substance undergoing transformation</term> has been spiritually elevated, it cannot reach the highest degrees of its perfection except through *fixation* <term>fixatio: the process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to fire</term>. This is because its *sublimation* <term>sublimatio: the process of vaporizing and purifying a substance</term>, which serves its exaltation and ascension, cannot be repeated with greater glory unless it is progressively fixed by bringing it back "from heaven to earth." Therefore, after its elevation, it must always be fixed, so that after a repeated elevation—which follows its fixation in sequence—it may be able to obtain the highest degrees of *glorification*. Through this glory, other "dead" substances <note>The author refers to "dead" base metals that lack the "life" or "spirit" of gold.</note> may afterwards be perpetually resurrected by it. If you recognize these things, you will understand the resurrection of Jesus Christ <note>original: "resurrectionem J. C."</note>, through which the guilty are made whole. Thus, the Philosopher wishes the sublimated stone to descend from heaven to earth.

Therefore, let the stone that was sublimated above be taken and placed in its sublimatory vessel, first by applying a very slow fire 
<meta>catchword: from</meta>

---

<page-num>257</page-num>
<header>The Purest Revelation</header>

from the ashes <note>An "ash fire" refers to a method of indirect heating where the vessel is buried in hot ashes to maintain a gentle, even temperature.</note> until nothing more rises through such a color; secondly, you shall give a stronger fire, from degree to degree, until whatever was volatile is sublimated from it. In this way, repeat the sublimation of the volatile part over the fixed part until that volatile part itself is likewise fixed. From here, *soften* <term>incera: "to wax," a process of adding liquid to a dry substance until it has the consistency of wax</term> it with its own "white oil," just as was described above concerning the fixation of the "second degree of air."

And in this way, you shall possess the glory of the brightness of the whole world, and all obscurity, poverty, and sickness shall flee from you. This is because the Stone is a cure for all illnesses, for it is "the strong strength of all strength" <note>original: "totius fortitudinis fortitudo fortis"; this is a direct reference to the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus.</note>. There is no comparison between this Stone and any other strengths of this world, because it conquers every subtle thing and penetrates every solid thing. It converts mercury, which is subtle, and perfects other solid bodies by penetrating them without limit.

### By Analogy Regarding the Red Work <note>original: "A Simili de Rubeo." The "Red Work" or Rubedo is the final stage of the alchemical process, representing the perfection of the Stone.</note>

Just as was stated regarding the white stone, you shall do for the red: namely, by dissolving the red stone in its own red water for three days in a cold place—that is, without heat—and in this way allow it to putrefy <term>putrefieri: the stage of "blackness" or decay where the substance breaks down to be reborn</term>.

Then, first separate the water by means of a water-bath <term>balneum: a vessel placed in hot water, like a modern bain-marie, to provide gentle heat</term>; afterward, separate the oil by means of an ash-fire <note>original: "per cineres" - using hot ashes to provide a steady, dry heat</note>, repeating this until nothing of the "soul" <note>the volatile spirit</note> remains in the "body" <note>the solid matter</note>, and the "earth" remains dry without any moisture, and becomes red as blood.

Afterward, by the method already described, join it with its simple, red, and non-fixed water, and sublime <term>sublimatio: vaporizing a solid into a gas and back to solid to purify it</term> it in turns—grinding and subliming—until on the second or third attempt the whole substance has been raised up. Then, by the previously mentioned method of fixation, fix it so that it remains stable; from here, wax it <term>incera: "inceration," the process of adding liquid to a dry powder until it has the consistency of wax and melts without smoke</term> with the red oil, just as you waxed the white stone.

Nor should any wise person ever wonder if such a "spirit," so highly purified and refined, transforms the body of a metal: even though the "earth" <note>the heavy, physical material</note> dominates in the quantity of the matter. For that matter is now 

<column-break/>

digested and refined, and treated for the operations of spirits, and therefore it follows their action and motion.

Furthermore, although even a tiny portion of this medicine is the smallest of things, it nevertheless contains within itself many powers of qualities to perform wonders, as is evident in the "projections" <term>projectiones: the act of casting the alchemical medicine onto a base metal to transform it into gold or silver</term>.

O natural purity of the soul! If you have not been polluted by any external filth, you are the fountain and origin of virtue. Here the elixir is called the "soul," because its entire substance has been converted into oil and gum.

### Concerning the multiplications of the medicines. <term>multiplicatio: the process of increasing the quantity and transformative power of the Alchemical Stone</term>

For the more often you repeat the operations of this third degree, the more the power of the medicines will be multiplied ten thousandfold. For instance, if the medicine is first cast over 1,000, the second time it converts ten thousand, because in each of its dissolutions it acquires ten [parts] in projection—wherefore ten times ten makes a hundred—and in each resolution through the elements it acquires ten times a hundred, which is a thousand. And in each spiritualization <note>the process of making a solid substance volatile or "spirit-like" through heat</note> toward the nature of heaven, it acquires ten thousand, and in the third [repetition] over a million <note>original: "mille millia" — literally a thousand thousands</note>, and thus through reiteration, the multiplication runs toward infinity over infinite thousands.

Therefore, the more you repeat the aforesaid operations, the more its power will be multiplied ten by ten. And in this indeed is completed the most precious secret <note>original: "arcanum pretiosissimum"</note>, which is an invaluable prize above the secrets of this world, and the treasure of all the Philosophers.

# Philosophers' Mastery

...with a recent preparation; and just as you did in the **mortification** <note>Mortification: In alchemy, this refers to the chemical breakdown or 'killing' of a substance, often resulting in a black color or loss of its original properties, intended to prepare it for a new form.</note> of the substances of the first degree, act in the same way in the second degree, until the entire matter remains mortified. ### On the generation of white sulfur from the union of two bodies.

The generation of this <term>stone</term> <note>original: "lapis"</note> should be similar to how other generations occur in nature, except that this one is made from three "natures" that have been more highly altered, processed, cooked, and greatly purified: namely, from <term>fixed red sulfur</term>, <term>unfixed white quicksilver</term> <note>Quicksilver: Mercury. Alchemists distinguished between "fixed" (solid/stable) and "unfixed" (volatile/vaporous) states.</note>, and a white body. 

But because no generation can happen without <term>putrefaction</term> <note>Putrefaction: The stage of chemical decay or 'blackening' (nigredo), which alchemists believed was a necessary death before the matter could be reborn in a purified state.</note>, and the <term>putrefaction of seeds</term> cannot occur unless they are cast into the earth as if into a womb, so neither can <term>our quicksilver</term> nor <term>sulfur</term> be changed or improved unless they are first cast into their dry "earth," which has been properly prepared and freed from all bad humors. And this is the <term>white earth</term> <note>original: "terra alba"</note>, well-purified and well-<term>calcined</term> <note>Calcine: To heat a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a fine powder or "ash."</note>, in which the two seeds mentioned before, when cast in as is fitting, are congealed, putrefied, divided, washed, they die, and 

<column-break/>

are corrupted, increased, and fermented, nourished, and multiplied.

Therefore, with God's blessing, let three parts of the white body be taken, and with one part of the <term>calcined</term> and fixed red body, let the powders <note>original: "calces"</note> be mixed by means of <term>imbibitions</term> <note>Imbibition: The process of adding a liquid to a solid so that it is absorbed, similar to a plant taking in water.</note>. This is done by soaking those powders with "white water," drop by drop <note>original: "roricè" - dew-like</note>, grinding them until no water is visible and the matter is mortified into a powder. Afterwards, the moisture of the imbibition should be removed over a very slow fire, and thus the moisture of the <term>quicksilver</term> recedes—yet in such a way that the whole substance of the <term>quicksilver</term> does not evaporate away.

Afterward, soak the aforementioned earth again as before, by grinding and cooking, and evaporating the excess moisture until all the water has been dried and mortified, and made white and shining through the strengthening of the fire of <term>calcination</term> and the drying of the water. Afterward, soak the calcined earth again, until it has "drunk up" a fiftieth part of its own weight of its water, as is stated below in the following chapter on the <term>sublimation of the earth</term> <note>Sublimation: Heating a solid until it becomes a vapor and then reverts to a solid in a purified form, often described as the "ascent" of the spirit.</note>.

### Concerning the vessels necessary for the Philosophical work.

Although many Philosophers have said that many vessels are necessary for this work, two alone are sufficient: namely, the <term>matrass</term> <note>original: "matratium" — A glass flask with a round body and a long neck.</note> and the <term>aludel</term> <note>original: "aludellum" — A pear-shaped pot or condenser used in the process of sublimation.</note>. But even though many people have used many other vessels, the entire work is completed in these two.

# The Mastery of the Philosophers

The first vessel in which the dissolutions of metals and their reductions into mercury take place through the first <term>putrefaction</term> <note>original: "putrefactionem" — A stage of decomposition where the substance "dies" and turns black before being reborn.</note>—at the beginning of the work after the preparation of the mercury—is called a <term>matrass</term> <note>original: "matratium" — A long-necked glass flask used for boiling and distilling.</note>, and it is marked with the letter **A**.

Another vessel is called an <term>aludel</term> <note>original: "aludellum" — A series of pear-shaped pots or tubes used to collect vapors during sublimation.</note>, which is divided into three parts. The first and most important part is the <term>cupel</term> <note>original: "copella" — Here referring to a shallow base-vessel or dish.</note>, which is made in the manner of a glass lamp; in this cupel, the dissolved and purified materials are cooked and <term>mortified</term> <note>original: "mortificantur" — The process of "killing" a substance by stripping away its outward qualities.</note>. This cupel is marked with the letter **B**.

The second part of this aludel vessel consists of a large cover which must fit into the cupel as far as the stop-rim, so that the material is covered by this lid. It must be sealed to the cupel with <term>paper lute</term> <note>original: "luto chartaceo" — A sealing paste made of clay mixed with paper fibers or linen to prevent it from cracking when heated.</note>. Within this cover, the thicker parts of the spirits are <term>sublimated</term> <note>original: "sublimantur" — The process where a solid turns into vapor and then solidifies again at the top of the vessel.</note> and raised, clinging to the sides of the cover. However, this cover must be perforated at the top in the manner of a funnel with a short neck, and this cover is marked with the letter **C**.

<column-break/>

# The Purest Revelation

The other part of this vessel is a small cover, positioned so that the fourth part of the large cover is protected by it. There, the small cover should be sealed. This cover must not be perforated at the top, where the more subtle spirits are raised and separated from the thicker ones; these pass through the hole of the large cover, enter the small cover, and tend upward, remaining there. For this reason, the small cover must not be perforated, but must be perfectly sealed to the large one with paper lute, so that the subtle nature does not evaporate. This small cover is marked with the letter **D**.

From these three parts joined together, the complete vessel called the <term>aludel</term> is made. In this vessel, <term>sublimations</term>, <term>distillations</term>, <term>coagulations</term>, as well as <term>mortifications</term> and essential <term>putrefactions</term> can be performed. However, in the case of essential putrefaction, the perforated lid is not necessary; rather, the small cover is sufficient, in which the more subtle parts are raised to the summit...

...they adhere to the top. In this vessel, however, the <term>resurrection of the dead</term> <note>original: "resurrectio mortuorum" — A metaphorical term for the stage where a substance is "reborn" in a purified, spiritualized state after decomposition.</note> and <term>calcination</term> <note>original: "calcinatio" — The process of reducing a substance to a fine powder or ash through prolonged heating.</note> can occur. The beginning of this work is to extract the mercury from Jupiter <note>original: "Iove" — In alchemy, Jupiter is the planetary name for the metal Tin.</note>, and to mix it with common prepared mercury, so that a <term>harmonic decoction</term> <note>original: "decoctio harmonica" — A balanced, rhythmic heating or "cooking" process designed to unite disparate substances into a single, stable whole.</note>, or a natural conjunction without separation, may be achieved.

### *Concerning the method of extracting the mercury of Jupiter.*

This mercury is extracted in various ways: but the best method is to take <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>original: "sal ammoniacum" — Ammonium chloride, a pungent salt highly valued by alchemists for its ability to help metals melt and for its role in the "revivification" of spirits.</note> in which a great power of revivification lies hidden, because Jupiter is nothing other than mercury coagulated by a certain earthy and impure sulfur; and this sulfur is not natural to it, but accidental, which ought to be removed from the matter of Jupiter by means of the <term>Art</term> <note>Alchemists frequently referred to their practice as "the Art" (Ars), implying a combination of technical skill and divine inspiration.</note>. And when this sulfur

### *The beginning of the work after the preparation of the aforementioned mercury.*

When the preparation of the mercury is finished, the work begins. ## The second decoction follows, through which the variation of color occurs.

Take this black powder <note>original: "pulverem nigrum" — the result of the first stage of heating described on the preceding page.</note> and grind it upon a marble slab. Once ground, place it in another vessel and join with the powder four ounces of the said prepared <term>mercury</term> <note>The "mercury" here refers to the purified metallic essence extracted from tin (Jupiter) or lead (Saturn) described earlier in the manuscript.</note>. Place your vessel in the furnace after <term>sealing</term> <note>original: "sigillationem" — likely a hermetic seal using clay or glass fusing to prevent the escape of vapors.</note> the vessel. Then, close up the furnace just as was said above regarding the first decoction, and similarly administer the fire for a space of 40 days. When the days are completed, allow the furnace to cool as before. Afterward, you must open the furnace and take the glass in which the powders are kept; there you will find the entire matter turned into a powder of a <term>russet</term> <note>original: "burelli" — a dark, brownish-red or greyish color, named after a type of coarse woolen cloth.</note> color, and this is the second decoction.

## Concerning the third decoction.

Take this powder, therefore, and grind it as before. Place it in the glass with seven ounces of the said mercury, seal the vessel, and place it in the furnace. Close the furnace as has been said, and administer the fire for 40 days,

<column-break/>

<page-num>313</page-num>
<header>The Work of Jupiter.</header>

and when this is done, allow it to cool. Upon opening the vessel afterward, you shall have a powder the color of ashes.

## Concerning the fourth decoction.

Take the powder and grind it, and join with it ten ounces of the said mercury. Once these are added, seal the glass and place it in the furnace. Close the furnace and <term>decoct</term> <note>original: "decoque" — to cook or heat intensely over a long period to concentrate the essence.</note> it with the fire and for the time already mentioned. When this is finished, allow the furnace to grow cold and break the glass; you will find a powder the color of flour <note>original: "farinae" — indicating a transition to a white or off-white stage.</note>. Thus the fourth decoction is completed.

## Concerning the fifth and final decoction.

This decoction is nothing other than a reiteration of the fourth decoction, using the same regimen of fire and time, and adding the said mercury to the ground powder. When the decoction is finished, break the glass and take the powder, which you will find to be the color of crystal. Keep this powder, therefore, with great care, because the work is complete.
