### *On the purification of Jupiter for fermentation.*

**T**ake the finest <term>tin</term> <note>original: "stanni" — In alchemy, Jupiter is the planetary name for the metal tin.</note> and melt as much of it as you wish. Once melted, quench it in a good <term>lye</term> made from the ashes of vine-shoots. Then melt it again, and pour the molten metal into a vessel full of ashes. Melt it a third time and pour it into a vessel full of <term>rock alum</term> <note>original: "aluminis rupium" — potassium aluminum sulfate, used here as a purifying agent.</note>, and let the alum be well-crushed. Do this two or three times in each material so that the metal is thoroughly purified. Then melt it once more and spread the molten metal out upon a clean table so that it becomes a thin plate.

### *On the fermentation of the powder.*

**T**ake one ounce of the crystalline powder and place it in a large earthen crucible. Then, join it immediately with three ounces of prepared mercury. Afterward, take six ounces of the tin purified as described above and melt it. When it has been melted, place it while still hot into the aforementioned earthen vessel, and immediately seal it carefully so that nothing escapes as smoke. Afterward, place the said vessel upon large glowing coals,

<column-break/>

and increase the fire as much as you can, yet let it be sufficient to heat the matter well. Let the vessel be surrounded by the fire so that the coals touch the vessel, and continue this fire for 4 hours. Then remove the vessel from the fire and allow it to cool. Once cooled, take what you find inside and save it carefully. When you wish to work with this matter for the <term>multiplication</term> <note>The process of increasing the quantity or potency of the alchemical "medicine" or Stone.</note> of medicines, proceed as follows, and note that the entire ferment will be converted into medicine.

### *On the multiplication of medicines.*

**T**ake these ten ounces of this medicine which has now been fermented, and add eight or ten ounces of prepared tin, and melt them together in a crucible. You will then have 18 or 20 ounces of the medicine, according to the amount added. Thus it will be enough to join one part with an equal part, and the whole will become the medicine: because the powder, already altered by the addition, alters the other material and converts it into its own nature, just like the <term>leaven</term> <note>original: "fermentum" — the author uses the analogy of yeast or sourdough starter (leaven) to explain how a small amount of alchemical medicine transforms a larger mass of metal.</note> of dough; the dough not yet raised into leaven... <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "mentum," part of the word "fermentum."</note>

### On the projection of this medicine.

Take ten ounces of this medicine, or ferment, and one ounce of <term>silver leaf</term> <note>original: "argenti foliati" — very thin sheets of silver, here used as a 'seed' to give the medicine the specific quality of silver.</note>, dissolved in prepared mercury, and cook the whole together in a <term>crucible</term> <note>original: "crucibulo" — a ceramic or metal container used for melting materials at very high temperatures.</note> for 4 hours: first with a gentle fire, second with a stronger fire, and third with the strongest fire, so that the whole melts together. This will become a medicine of which one ounce is projected upon ten ounces of the finest tin, and the whole will become a medicine to be projected upon seven pounds of the said tin, and the whole will become the finest silver. And this occurs because of the purification and the cooking of the materials, and the excellently purified ferment, because the extreme purification of one thing cleanses and purifies another.

## *When the medicine can be taken up for making the projection.*

It should also be noted that at the end of 4 months, the third <term>decoction</term> <note>original: "decoctio" — the process of boiling or heating a substance in a liquid to extract its essence or change its properties.</note> ends, and then the powder is reduced to the color of dead ashes. Of this powder, as I have said, one ounce is projected upon ten of purified tin, and a ferment is made which you must join with one ounce of dissolved silver, as was said.

And when the medicine is the color of flour, it can be taken up at the end of 5 and a half months, and one should work just as described.

And when the medicine is in the color of crystal, you can take it up at the end of seven months; and as was established and written regarding its multiplication, with the addition of the silver ferment having been made, work with them, and then project it upon the said quantity of tin.

### *Here begins another method for changing Jupiter into Luna.*

Extinguish <term>Jupiter</term> <note>original: "Iovem" — the alchemical name for the metal Tin.</note> when melted in the lime-water of eggshells, then in alum water, and finally extinguish it in very strong vinegar: so that it loses its <term>creaking</term> <note>original: "stridorem" — refers to the "cry of tin," a characteristic crackling sound produced when the metal is bent.</note> and achieves an easy melting. Take this and <term>amalgamate</term> <note>To combine a metal with mercury to form a paste-like alloy.</note> it with an equal quantity of mercury that has been very well washed and prepared through sublimation. Afterward, wash it with common water and prepared common salt: then rinse the amalgam with hot water so that no salt remains there, and thus clarify the matter well, and afterward dry it. When these things are finished, sublime the whole amalgam through a <term>retort</term> <note>A glass or ceramic vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation.</note>, first with a moderate fire for the space of one hour: then increase the fire a little, and finally let it be made strong, and then strongest of all, so that the mercury may be separated from the tin. Once it is separated, wash the mercury and dry it, and pass the mercury through a filter, and again amalgamate it with the tin remaining in the bottom of the vessel; wash and cleanse it as before with water and salt, and extract the saltiness by means of hot water, and again

<column-break/>

sublime it again in the retort, so that the mercury is separated from the tin, and repeat this seven times: finally, add and melt with it an equal part of <term>Luna</term> <note>original: "lunæ" — the alchemical name for Silver.</note>, and pass the tin and silver through a <term>cupel</term> <note>original: "copellam" — a small, porous bowl used in refining to separate precious metals from base metals.</note>, and almost the whole will be the best silver.

### *In another way.*

If the best silver is added at the beginning and the whole is made into an amalgam: wash this amalgam, and separate the mercury from the tin and silver through the aforementioned sublimation: this will happen more quickly and powerfully, because the silver hardens the tin excellently when they have been amalgamated together. Wash and dry the separated mercury; afterward take what remains in the bottom of the vessel and grind it into a powder, and again let an amalgam be made of these with the washed mercury. Cook the amalgam with a gentle fire in an <term>aludel</term> <note>original: "aludello" — a series of pear-shaped pots used as receivers in the sublimation process.</note> for 24 hours; afterward grind what remains in the bottom, and cast it upon a fourth part of melted silver, and the whole will be the best silver.

### Another method.

Melt the finest tin, purified as has been said at the best <term>moon</term> <note>original: "luna optima" — likely refers to performing the work when the Moon is in a favorable astrological position, though it could also imply the presence of silver.</note>, and the whole thing will become a dry paste. Reduce this paste into the finest filings, and cast the material—namely the hot filings—into hot mercury. Specifically, use one ounce of filings for every 8 ounces of mercury, and thus an <term>amalgam</term> <note>A blend of mercury with another metal.</note> will be made. You must wash this until the whole thing is very clear and shining; afterward, <term>sublime</term> <note>To heat a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, used here to separate the mercury.</note> it with a gentle fire as much as can be sublimed, and increase the fire little by little every six hours until nothing more can rise into the <term>aludel</term> <note>original: "aludellum" — a series of earthenware pots used as condensers in the sublimation process.</note>. Then, melt the material left in the bottom, and it will be perfect silver.

### For turning Jupiter into Silver:

Take a certain quantity of the matter of <term>Jupiter</term> <note>Tin.</note> and <term>calcine</term> <note>To heat a substance to a high temperature in air, reducing it to a powder or "calx."</note> it strongly in a crucible, stirring it constantly with an iron spatula until the entire material is turned into powder, and let it be a most precise powder. Dissolve this powder in prepared mercury that has been purified of all filth, and grind it until the whole thing is reduced into a paste—

<column-break/>

—[reduced]. In another batch of mercury, also prepared, you must dissolve a fourth part of the finest <term>Luna</term> <note>Silver.</note>; that is, dissolve a fourth part of silver—namely one ounce—in the prepared mercury, and let them be like a soft paste, passed however through a linen cloth. Then, evaporate the mercury gently so that the silver may be calcined; collect what has risen and keep it aside. Then increase the fire and evaporate the remaining mercury dwelling in the silver, and continue thus until you have a <term>calx of silver</term> <note>The powdery metallic ash remaining after silver has been heated or chemically treated.</note>. You must calcine this silver calx strongly for 12 hours in an earthen crucible, and let the crucible always be white-hot, but take care that the silver does not melt.

Therefore, take this calx and <term>imbibe</term> <note>To soak or saturate a dry substance with a liquid.</note> it with the mercury of dissolved Jupiter <note>The tin-mercury mixture prepared in the first column.</note> so that the solution may be <term>mortified</term> <note>original: "mortificetur" — to 'kill' or change the outward metallic form of a substance, a necessary step in its transformation.</note>. Afterward, cook this mortified material for 4, 5, or 6 days; then grind the material and reduce it to powder, and repeat the imbibition and cooking until the entire material is reduced to powder.

Afterward, melt silver in a crucible, and cast this powder into the said molten silver, but do so bit by bit; and the whole will be converted into the finest silver.

## *On the multiplication of this medicine.*

Take one ounce of this <term>deadened powder</term> <note>original: "pulveris mortificati" — a substance that has undergone "mortification," a process intended to strip a material of its original outward properties or "volatility" to prepare it for transformation.</note>, already cooked with <term>lunar calx</term> <note>original: "calce lunaria" — silver that has been reduced to a powder or oxide through heat.</note>; and in four ounces of the said prepared mercury, dissolve this powder according to the art of dissolution, so that it is converted into mercury. Then, you must deaden it by the method I told you; afterward, cook it for 5 or 6 days so that the mercury becomes very hard, and finally grind it so that it becomes a most exact powder.

Afterward, take the powders and <term>imbibe</term> <note>To slowly add liquid to a dry substance so it is absorbed.</note> them again as before, and cook them as has been said until the entire matter is turned into powder. Cast this powder gradually upon other molten silver as was said above, and the whole thing will be a "fermented medicine," powerful enough to convert other mercury into silver. And in this way, you will be able to multiply the medicine of this material infinitely, both in its quantity and its power.

Therefore, keep some part of this medicine for performing the multiplication of medicines, and never be—

---

->The Work of Jupiter.<-

—destitute of it. Know therefore that one ounce should be sufficient for you, since it is a multiplicative medicine.

And just as you did with tin, the same can be done with lead. However, if you wish to work with lead, you must extract its mercury and purge it very well through the methods of the art, because it contains many impurities that cannot be separated without great labor, for it is far from the perfection of tin. Work therefore with tin if you wish to shorten the time, because it is closest to the nature of silver.

## *What Lead and Tin are composed of, and the difference between them.*

We have said before that all metals are composed of sulfur and mercury, and their diversity arises from the impurity or purity of these principles, as we shall see below.

### *On the nature of Lead, and on its composition.*

<term>Lead</term> <note>original: "Plumbum"</note> is the most imperfect metal of all, unclean and filthy, composed of an impure, earthy <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argento vivo" — mercury</note> that is not <term>fixed</term> <note>original: "non fixo" — in alchemy, a "fixed" substance is one that can withstand fire without evaporating or changing.</note>, and of foulness. In its manifest appearance it is a dull white, but in its hidden center it is red, and it is composed of a similar impure and earthy sulfur; in this metal, both purity and fixation are lacking.

### *On the nature of Tin, and on its composition.*

<term>Tin</term> <note>original: "Stannum"</note> is a bright metal, yet still imperfect, composed of pure quicksilver—partly fixed and partly not fixed. It is white and clear in its manifest appearance, but red in its hidden center, and composed of a similar sulfur. Nothing is lacking in it except <term>cooking and digestion</term> <note>original: "coctio & digestio" — the alchemical process of applying heat over time to "ripen" a metal into a more perfect state, like gold or silver.</note>. For this reason, it receives the form of silver more readily and suitably than <term>Saturn</term> <note>The alchemical name for Lead.</note>, which is otherwise called Lead.

<column-break/>

->The Work of Jupiter.<-

### *Why Lead is called Saturn and Tin is also called Jupiter.*

The ancient Philosophers gave the name of <term>Saturn</term> to lead because the virtues of this planet flow into it with stronger forces than those of the other planets at the time of its production or generation, and during the <term>coagulation</term> <note>The process of a liquid becoming solid.</note> and cooking of its mercury. And because the qualities of this planet, which are cold and earthy, flow into it, this metal shares in the nature of Saturn much more than other metals do.

The same occurs in the production or generation of tin, into which the virtues and qualities of <term>Jupiter</term> flow; for this reason, these metals receive the names of these planets.

And because it is said in the <term>Assembly of the Philosophers</term> <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum" — one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, presented as a debate between pre-Socratic philosophers.</note> that one metal always contains another in its center, and that within one single metal all others are truly contained—which is called quicksilver. And because all metals are of the same metallic nature, which is called sulfur and mercury by the Philosophers: therefore, they can [be changed] mutually, one into another...

### For extracting Mercury from all metals.

First, take the metal from which you wish to extract mercury; according to the art, reduce this metal into a <term>lime</term> <note>original: "calcem" — a powdered oxide or residue produced by heating a metal in air</note>; Afterward, dissolve common <term>decrepitated salt</term> <note>Salt that has been heated until it stops crackling, used to remove moisture</note> in common <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>original: "aqua forti" — literally "strong water," which is nitric acid</note>, and dissolve it little by little until the aqua fortis can no longer dissolve any more. ### On Simple Virgin Milk.

Simple **virgin milk** is nothing other than the **essence of the moon** <note>original: "essentia lunae" — referring to the refined spirit of Silver</note> for the white work, and the **essence of the sun** <note>original: "essentia solis" — the refined spirit of Gold</note> for the red work. Furthermore, prepared mercury in which silver has been dissolved and reduced back into mercury is also called virgin milk. In short: both are made from the substance of a perfect metal, and both provide the power of <term>tinging</term> <note>the ability of the alchemical agent to transform the color and nature of a base metal</note>. However, this milk is not a solvent itself, but is the dissolved substance of perfect metals which is never separated from the **Elixir**. Instead, the solvent is separated from the substance itself by means of fire, just as rainwater is separated from the earth by the heat of the sun, leaving behind the "celestial substance," which is the nourishment for all fruits that remain in the earth.

### Another secret for converting Mercury into Silver.

Take 8 ounces of **mercury** <note>quicksilver</note> sublimated with **lime** and **tartar**, and three parts of **leaf silver** <note>original: "lunæ foliatæ" — silver beaten into thin sheets</note>; let an **amalgam** be made by mixing them together. ### *A perennial and artificial mine, for the red work.* <note>original: "ad rubeum" — referring to the Rubedo, the final red stage of the alchemical process to create gold</note>

Take **calcined gold** <note>gold reduced to a fine powder through heat or chemical action</note>, and dissolve it in the best prepared **mercury**; place it in a very strong fire within a **Philosophical vessel** <note>a specialized glass flask, often called a Pelican or a Hermetic vase</note>, and let the vessel be buried in ashes for 40 days. However, you must seal the vessel **hermetically** <note>sealed air-tight by melting the glass of the neck</note>. When the days have passed, all the gold will be converted into mercury. Sublime this mercury very gently, and save what rises to the top, for it is the **dissolving water** <note>original: "aqua dissolutiva"</note>. Increase the fire, and whatever remains at the bottom, **fix** <note>to turn a volatile substance into a solid that can withstand fire</note> by the method of **fixation**—namely, by ascending and descending in the Philosophical vessel—until the whole is fixed. Afterward, **calcine** it. Take this **lime** <note>original: "calcem" — the powdery residue left after heating</note> and incorporate it with mercury, using an equal weight of mercury. Just as you did before, fix this mercury, continuing this operation until the whole has been fixed. And if you run out of **animated mercury** <note>mercury "given life" or essence by the spirit of gold</note>, the same can be done with common mercury; in this way, the powder increases infinitely. This powder can easily be reduced back into running and living mercury, and it will be animated mercury,

### *What is first necessary in the secrets of minerals.*

In the first place, therefore, one must strive above all to have the greatest abundance of the purest **radical volatile part** <note>original: "volatilis mineralium partis radicalis" — the fundamental, "root" essence or spirit of the mineral</note> of minerals, free from all contamination. ### *On the multiplication of the mineral medicine.*

Take the fermented earth and dissolve it in its own water according to the art of dissolution <note>original: "dissolutionis artem" — the chemical process of turning a solid into a liquid state</note>, filter the solution, and through distillation with a gentle fire, dry the earth: and always collect the distilled water diligently, so that you do not run out of water: and you will have a medicine multiplied in power. In this way, you will be able to multiply the medicine unto infinity.

### *The First Method.*

Take eight or ten parts of our **white vinegar**, and one part of the finest **gold** <note>original: "solis" (the Sun) — the standard alchemical symbol for gold</note> of our mother: let these last two be reduced into a **calx** <term>calx: the crumbly, oxidized powder resulting from the heating or chemical dissolution of a metal</term> by the Philosophical way, or if you prefer, by **aqua fortis** <note>literally "strong water," the historical name for nitric acid, used to dissolve metals</note>, or another method.

Let the whole calx be amalgamated with the white vinegar: let it stand in a slow heat for 21 days. Let the vinegar be poured off from the matter: and let the matter be advanced to the second degree of fire until a blackness appears. This will happen within about a month. Now let the **Philosophers' Egg** <note>a round glass vessel with a long neck, designed to be hermetically sealed for the "digestion" of the alchemical matter</note> be opened, the matter being coagulated

### Another secret for multiplying the Sun. <note>In alchemical texts, "the Sun" (Sol) refers to Gold</note>

Take one ounce of the best gold leaf <note>original: "Solis foliati"</note>, and four ounces of the best mercury <note>quicksilver</note> prepared according to the art; let them be mixed together, and let an **amalgam** <term>amalgam: a soft or liquid alloy made by mixing mercury with another metal, often used as a starting point for metallic transformations</term> be made. Let it be placed in a gentle, warm sun until the amalgam hardens. Then take as much decrepitated common salt <note>original: "salis communis decrepitati" — table salt that has been heated until it stops crackling or "popping," a process used to remove moisture and prevent the vessel from shattering during high-heat operations</note> as the amalgam weighs. Mix them together by grinding and enclose them in a sublimation vessel. Distill by means of an ash bath <note>original: "per cineres" — a method of heating a vessel evenly by nesting it in a container of hot ashes</note> with a very strong fire in the manner of a sublimation, and continue the fire until the volatile material is separated from the gold. That which remains at the bottom of the vessel must be washed with common warm water until it no longer tastes of salt; afterwards dry it, and melt it, and let it—

—be melted alone, and you will find your gold multiplied from the fixable substance of the mercury—namely, by one drachm per ounce.    Therefore, amalgamate and cook <note>original: "decoque" — to boil down or heat intensely</note> as was said: namely, until the material hardens. Afterwards, mix the material with decrepitated common salt, grinding and mixing well, and then sublimating until the volatile is separated from the fixed. Then wash it as before, so that all the salt is separated by the warm water and the material is sweetened <note>original: "dulcificetur" — the alchemical process of removing corrosive salts or acids by washing, making the substance chemically neutral or "sweet"</note>; afterward let it be dried and melted. And thus you will easily have the increase.

### Preparation or the first operation.

The dissolution of the body is the foundation of the art, and this dissolution is the reduction of the body into water: specifically into <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum vivum," literally "living silver" or mercury</note>, and this is called "solution." Hence the Philosophers have said: Let the gold which is hidden in the body of magnesia <note>original: "magnesiæ" — in alchemy, this refers to a primitive or raw mineral substance, not modern magnesium</note> be dissolved, and let it be reduced into its first matter, so that it may become <term>true sulfur</term> and <term>quicksilver</term>. For our solution is nothing other than the body returning to a liquid state, being resolved into the nature of quicksilver, and the saltiness of its sulfur being diminished—which divine sulfur is made from two sulfurs when it encounters the body.

### Preparation or the second operation.

The water passes into the body; for one is not dissolved unless the other is congealed, because the body of the quicksilver, con-
<meta>catchword: ceiving</meta>

---

<header>of the Philosophers.</header>

ceiving, coagulates itself, and is coagulated by the body, and becomes earth.

This is the **second word** of this work, of which the Greek Philosophers spoke. Water is procreated from earth, because water becomes earth when the qualities of earth prevail in it; and earth becomes water when the qualities of water prevail in it.

For the dissolution of the body and the coagulation of the spirit occur so that they may have one single operation, and become one thing, to which nothing foreign is added—except that in the preparation, superfluous things are removed with the proper equipment. And this is dissolution and <term>coagulation</term> <note>the process of turning a liquid into a solid or semi-solid state</note>, from which follows drying <note>original: "desiccatio"</note>, and finally <term>calcination</term> <note>heating a substance to a high temperature to reduce it to a powder or "ash"</note>.

### Preparation and the third operation:

The earth is plowed and watered, joined, and by the will of God, it is directed in the water. This is the **third word** of this work.

The Philosophers say: this earth rots <note>original: "putrescit" — putrefaction was considered a vital stage of breaking down matter to allow for new growth</note> with water and is purified. Then, with the help of God, the mastery <note>original: "magisterium" — the "Great Work" or the secret process of creating the Philosophers' Stone</note> is directed or continued along the right path, because

### The Fifth Preparation and Operation.

Our spirit is the carrier of the soul's virtues, because our brass <note>original: "æs" — here referring to the base alchemical matter or the "body" being worked upon</note> has a body, spirit, and soul, just as a human does.

This is the fifth word of this work, about which the Philosophers say: its spirit is water, its soul is the tincture <note>original: "tinctura" — the transforming power or the essence that grants color</note>, and its body is earth. Yet the spirit is a spirit just as the body is the bond of the soul itself; thus the body is fixed, dry, and contains the spirit and soul. Therefore, the spirit penetrates the body; the body fixes the spirit; the soul joins them together, whitens, and dyes them with its own color, whether white or red.

### The Sixth Preparation.

It varies and changes from color to color, until it reaches the goal of whiteness and redness.

As long as moisture dominates, the matter turns black, because heat acting upon the moist generates blackness first; but acting upon the dry, it generates whiteness; and in the white, it generates a yellow color <note>original: "citrinitatem"</note>, just as appears in lead from which minium <note>original: "minium" — red lead or lead tetroxide, a red pigment produced by heating lead white</note> is made. The King, crowned with a diadem, cries out: "I am the white son of the black, and the Red son of the whiteness, and I do not lie." <note>original: "Ego sum albus filius nigri, & Rubens filius albedinis" — a classic alchemical riddle describing the progression from the black stage (nigredo) to the white stage (albedo) and finally the red stage (rubedo).</note> And therefore the Philosophers say: cook them until they become black, then white, then yellow-citrine, and finally let it become a staining poison <note>original: "tingens venenum" — in alchemy, 'poison' often refers to a potent, transformative elixir that 'attacks' and changes the nature of metals.</note>; because the more they are cooked, the more they are dissolved and blackened; and the more they are cooked, the more they are dried and whitened; thirdly, the more they are cooked, the more they are reddened until they are perfected.

Truly, he who errs through ignorance in these matters will very often weep over his downfall. ### *The Seventh Arrangement or Operation.*

The blessed stone <term>lapis benedictus</term> is multiplied and perfected when the unfixed <note>original: "non fixa" — the volatile or vaporous part of the matter</note> amount is fixed with it until it flows.

This is the seventh word of this work, about which the Philosophers say: Now you must make the fixed stone volatile <note>original: "volatilem" — able to rise as a vapor</note> by means of sublimation, in a philosophical manner, joining them through the smallest parts <note>original: "per minima" — referring to the fundamental particles or the most subtle level of matter</note>, so that the entire subtle substance is raised in the vessel, and then it shall be fixed. If this does not happen, let a quantity of the unfixed part be added to it, so that the volatile part exceeds the total of the fixed part until it is sufficient for its elevation, by repeating the process. For if the volatile overcomes the amount of the fixed, the volatile is fixed with it; if it does not overcome but is overcome, it becomes volatile. Therefore, let the amount of the fixed be repeated with that which was elevated; however, after the turn, until the whole is fixed by this sublimation and repetition of the matter. When, however, the whole has been fixed, repeat the unfixed part also; yet absorb it quantity by quantity through the skill known to you, until the whole is raised; and finally, by repeating, let it be fixed until it provides an easy fusion in the manner...

### *Paraphrase of the seventh preparation.*

This concerns the multiplication of the already perfected Stone, which is as follows:
The Stone, already fixed, must be exalted through mystical sublimation; <term>Sublimation</term> <note>In alchemy, sublimation often refers to the purification of a solid by heating it into a vapor and then condensing it back into a solid, but "mystical" sublimation implies a spiritual or higher energetic refinement.</note> that is, it must be increased in body and virtue through repeated operations of solutions and coagulations.

Take it, therefore, and in its vessel or glass, drench it with quicksilver <note>original: "argento vivo" — literally "living silver," the common term for mercury.</note> in such a way that you drop it in bit by bit and allow it to enter and penetrate the whole until the dryness is hidden and moisture now dominates, appearing clearly. And if it does not yet dominate, but dryness prevails, you must drop in more mercury, as much as suffices for [making it] volatile...

## *Note.*

Arnold <note>Likely referring to Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a celebrated physician and alchemist whose works were foundational to the field.</note> says that in the first <term>Projection</term> <note>The act of "casting" the finished Alchemical Stone or powder onto a base metal to achieve transmutation.</note> he does not produce gold from mercury, but instead produces a "medicine," which in turn gives birth to another medicine, and finally, on the third attempt, gold. But it is necessary then that the Stone has been <term>Exalted</term> <note>Refined or increased in potency.</note> through repeated operations, so that by the strength of its virtue it may seize the mercury and allow nothing to be scattered. When the powder is cast into boiling <term>Quicksilver</term> <note>Mercury.</note>, it begins to bubble and give off <term>popping sounds</term> <note>original: "poppyfmos," from the Greek *poppysmos*, describing a clicking, hissing, or smacking sound.</note>; but shortly after, it settles. Then, while it is in a state of flux, we burn powdered borax over it so that it may become beautiful gold. Then it is poured into a channel and transferred for use. One part ought to have transformed 1,000 parts, such that one grain would transform 16 drachmas and 40 grains. However, in this experiment, only 12 drachmas are produced. Therefore, it could have been exalted further if the practitioners had known the method.

It should also be noted that if the projection is to be made upon "bodies" <note>In alchemy, "bodies" refers to solid metals like lead, tin, or copper, as opposed to "spirits" like mercury.</note>, the Philosophers command that one must be careful that the Stone is not too subtle <note>In this context, "subtle" means so refined or ethereal that it lacks a physical affinity with the solid metal.</note> and thus foreign to the fellowship of the bodies. For it does not enter impure things, but floats on the

### The Washing of the Tartar, or Earth.

### On the conjunction of the two Luminaries <note>The "Luminaries" are the Sun and Moon, the alchemical symbols for Gold and Silver.</note>.

When you have the luminaries—namely the **Sun** <note>original: "fol" (sol), gold.</note> and the **Moon** <note>original: "luna," silver.</note>—prepared and reduced into oil, and afterwards fermented as has been described, join one ounce of the one with an equal weight of the other. Thus they will be reduced to a state of equality; that is, they will be neither toward the white nor toward the red, but will be neutral. Then, if you wish to make the **white**, ferment this composition with an equal part of white ferment; after fermentation, dissolve and coagulate it in such a way that the coagulum approaches <term>fixation</term> <note>The process by which a volatile substance is rendered stable under heat.</note>. Project one part onto one hundred parts of mercury, and it will be a medicine for projecting one part onto a hundred weights, and the whole will be the finest silver.

And as has been said of the white, so it is for the **red**.

If you wish to increase the strength or power of your medicines, you need do nothing else but dissolve, coagulate, and finally fix them. And the medicine will be multiplied unto infinity, and always [the] medicines...

...unless to their own sons who understand their words; I say indeed to those sons who work in the proper matter <note>original: "materia debita," the specific base material required for the Great Work.</note>, although they are very rare, since their intention is not at all understood according to the literal meaning: and thus such a literal intention is of no use.

To work according to the literal letter, however, is the destruction of wealth: and therefore **Geber** <note>Referring to the 13th-century Latin author known as "Pseudo-Geber," who wrote under the name of the 8th-century Persian polymath Jabir ibn Hayyan. For there are certain blind men, taught only how to **sublime**, who think themselves learned and yet understand nothing. Others know only how to **distill**, others to **calcine**; others only to **dissolve**, **coagulate**, and **fix**, and thus by this alone they think they know the whole <term>mastery</term> <note>original: "magisterium," the complete process or the finished Stone.</note>. Deceived in the end, they wander through the world until they can even deceive others; and because of their habits and deceptions, many call our most precious science a lie.

Nevertheless, the operations mentioned above should not be considered except in a double sense: for the Philosophers very often understood by **distillation** the separation of the thick from the subtle; and sometimes they called the clarification of materials "distillation," and they even call filtration "distillation."

And by **dissolution** they do not always mean reduction into water, but very often they understood it as the separation of one subject from another. So also by **sublimation** they do not always mean the raising of materials to the top of the vessel, but often by sublimation they understood the purification and the **exaltation** <note>The process of increasing the power or spiritual quality of a substance.</note> of virtues. And thus many do not understand the words of the Philosophers, and yet they usurp the title of "Philosopher."

But no one can grant themselves the name of Philosopher unless they first know all of nature; second, unless they know how nature acts in the **generation** of things; furthermore, unless they know what matter nature uses to nourish its children, and how all things grow through its nourishment; and why they increase in body and power, and are exalted, and finally destroyed, and then **regenerated**. Truly, whoever is able to know this can worthily take the title of Philosopher for themselves.

But since the Philosophers have said that **dissolution** is the foundation of the art, let us then see how we ought to understand the dissolution of medicines.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of alchemical operations, specifically moving from the general warnings against literal interpretation to a technical explanation of "solution" and "subtiliation." It bridges the gap between the theory of the "Sons of Art" and the practical transformation of matter.</meta>

<page-num>394</page-num>
# The Seven Words

Nevertheless, the **solution of medicines** is not a reduction into water, but merely the **subtiliation** <note>In alchemy, "subtiliation" refers to the process of refining a substance, making it "subtle" or ethereal, rather than simply dissolving it in a liquid.</note> of the parts that were joined and united during the **fixation** of the medicine; that is to say, they are separated and afterwards restored, so that the dry becomes moist, and the thick becomes simple, and vice-versa. For the solution of medicines is performed so that they may be more greatly refined, and so that the thick parts of the body may be better united, and so that the medicine may be brought, through solution, **from potentiality to actuality.** <note>original: "de potentia ad actum." This is an Aristotelian concept frequently used in alchemy: the substance has the "potential" to be the Philosopher's Stone, but the process of solution "activates" that power.</note>

Indeed, this is clear only to the experienced, because when bodies are refined, they are dissolved—that is, universally—and united with spirits **at the most minute level**, <note>original: "per minima." This refers to the union of substances at the smallest possible scale, similar to our modern concept of molecular or atomic bonding.</note> so that they cannot be separated from them by any sharpness of human wit. Therefore, he who separates the bodies by distilling during the first refinement or solution will achieve the desired end: because the entire intention of the worker ought to be in the **union of spirits**. This intention will never be fulfilled unless the body is in the same state of refinement as the spirit; and the body is made subtle in the manner of a spirit through **grinding** and **waxing**, <term>inceration</term> <note>original: "inceratio," the process of adding a liquid to a dry substance, drop by drop, until it takes on the consistency of soft wax.</note> or through its solution and **roasting** <note>original: "assationem," a slow heating process.</note> with its own spirit. In this way it is made subtle and not otherwise: because that which is subtle has the power to enter into matter,

<meta>catchword: and</meta>

What, therefore, is this smoky and white matter, thickened in the belly of the earth? ### *In these short discourses, the entire Mastery <note>original: "Magisterium." This refers to the "Great Work" or the complete process of alchemical transformation.</note> is revealed.*

If anyone desires the secret of God, let him descend into the **well of penitence** <note>original: "puteus pœnitentiæ." In alchemical literature, "penitence" or "humility" often metaphorically refers to the *nigredo* or blackening stage, where the matter must "die" or be humbled before it can be purified.</note>, in which our **blessed stone** <note>original: "lapis benedictus," another name for the Philosopher's Stone.</note> is found. For **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius." This is the philosophical Mercury, the universal spirit or "first matter" of all things.</note> is extracted from all things: and he who names the whole, excludes nothing: if therefore it is from all things:

Take the most noble Mercury, which by its great abundance is said to belong to one alone. Therefore, if anyone knows the way—which is unique—he descends into the well of penitence, and there he is set on fire; he who descends through such a practice will without doubt obtain the secret of God, according to the opinion of the true Philosopher. However, to know the method: *this is the work, this is the labor* <note>original: "hoc opus hic labor est," a famous quote from Virgil’s Aeneid regarding the difficulty of returning from the underworld.</note>. The investigation is difficult, yet the thing, once found, is easy: remember therefore that **man** is the most noble creature in the composition of the earth that God ever created, in whom there are **four Elements** proportioned by nature: from such a person, a "mercuriality" or "vitriolity" <note>original: "vitriolitas," referring to the acidic or transformative quality of Vitriol, a key alchemical substance.</note>, which is of no price, is produced by **Art** <note>original: "Arte," referring to the Alchemical Art.</note> from its own mineral.

This dryness overcomes the quality of its watery substance and dries it out, so that it becomes solid and firm, provided that the dryness prevails. This is the **coagulated and specified seed**, and the **first matter of metals** <note>original: "prima materia metallorum"</note>.

However, there is another specified seed that is not yet coagulated, which is also called the **quicksilver of the Philosophers**. It cannot be distinguished except by its liquid body, which is the spirit of common quicksilver. Yet this spirit is a metallic and generative power in which **dryness** is hidden; this is the **metallic natural moisture** <note>original: "humidum naturale metallicum"</note>. But as long as the superfluous wateriness of this quicksilver exists in the form of "metallic water," it has no form of salt, because of the excessive moisture—

---

# 411 of the Philosophers.

—overcoming its own <term>radical moisture</term> <note>The essential, life-sustaining fluid of a substance</note> and **radical dryness**. This matter is always **volatile** <note>tending to evaporate or escape into the air</note>. Therefore, this superfluous moisture must be separated. However, it can in no way be separated from its spirit or radical moisture unless we have this radical moisture already coagulated by nature and specified into a metal. We must join these together and, by means of **Art** <note>The alchemical process or craft</note>, turn them into the **quicksilver of the Philosophers**. Afterward, the dry nature—that is, the dry power—is found there; this dryness, by acting upon the superfluous moisture, separates it from the whole metallic substance through repeated operations.

Nevertheless, this dry, coagulated substance, already converted into the nature of a metal, has its own **metallic termination** <note>The final, fixed state of a metal's development</note>. This termination is its boundary, within which is contained the power of shaping and converting into metal.

And when the substance of this quicksilver is separated from the superfluous and watery substance by the predominating dryness, then the **mercury of the Philosophers** appears in a coagulated state, which is the spirit of common quicksilver. But if perhaps this quicksilver...

# 412 Seven Words

...common, and if it had no spirit, all of this **quicksilver** <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum vivum," also known as mercury</note> would be destroyed and turned into dross <note>original: "fæculentiam," referring to waste or impurities</note>. But our most noble quicksilver is coagulated and finally made permanent <note>original: "fixatur," a term for making a substance resistant to heat</note>, by means of quicksilver that has already been made permanent by nature and converted into a metal. Thus, its moist substance becomes dry by means of the dry quality dominating in the finished matter; and conversely, the dry becomes moist as the moist nature overcomes and dissolves it. 

Since this watery metallic substance is of the same kind as the coagulated, finished, and permanent substance, they must be joined together so that they can never be separated afterward. In this way, like attracts its like; the moist substance dissolves the coagulated one and purifies it, joining with its own **radical moisture** <note>original: "humido radicali," the essential, life-sustaining fluid of a substance</note>, and finally they become one. When this coagulated radical moisture, which has been reduced to a metal, has been dissolved, it is called the **quicksilver of the Philosophers**.

By these words and arguments, it has been sufficiently demonstrated to the intelligent reader that the Philosophers possess two kinds of quicksilver: one that is **volatile** <note>tending to evaporate or escape into the air</note> and another that is **fixed** <note>stable and resistant to fire</note>. But to answer all possible questions,

---

# 413 of the Philosophers.

we must understand that there are two kinds of volatile quicksilver: namely, one that is **universal** and another that is **specified**. The first takes the form of common water, while the second takes a metallic form, and both of these are volatile. The first has no form except a universal one and can be considered simply as the **first matter** <note>original: "materia prima," the primal substance from which all things are created</note> of all things not yet specified. The second, however, has a specific metallic form and yet is like a metallic water.

The last type is entirely metallic, which the Philosophers call **fixed**. This quicksilver is a **perfect metal**, which must be dissolved by other substances and reduced back to its original principles.

Because gold and other metals can be reduced into quicksilver by means of **dissolution**, the Philosophers call them "quicksilver" in view of their dissolution and "quicksilver" in view of their resolution. In the same way, they called volatile quicksilver "fixed" in view of its own fixed nature, which is contained in the center of its substance; for it is easily made permanent by means of a substance already fixed by nature and converted into a metal—

# *The First Epistle of Antonius de Abatia.*

WHEN I have seen many volumes written by the Philosophers <note>original: "Philosophis," the term used for alchemical masters of the past</note> regarding the **transmutation of metals**, yet they are so obscure that almost no one can understand them, owing to their language being weighed down with riddles: and although they have declared the truth in those works, they nevertheless demonstrated it only according to their own hidden intentions. Very often, amidst their most truthful words, they recited many trivialities, and they so hid and concealed essential matters in "thorny ground" <note>original: "terra spinosa," a metaphor for difficult, obscured, or confusing text</note> that they can be neither understood nor reached by anyone, unless they possess the sword of Alexander to cut the **Gordian knot** <note>A legendary knot that was impossible to untie, eventually cut by Alexander the Great; here, it refers to the decisive insight needed to solve alchemical mysteries</note>—that is, unless they resolve all the difficulties that arise.

Therefore, most dear friends and students of this art, I wished to warn you that you should not act, nor weary yourselves in reading or studying the books of the Philosophers concerning the **Chemical Art** <note>original: "Arte Chymica," alchemy</note>, since you will be able to find nothing clear there; for they wrote only for the wise and for those who...

Therefore, <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the Greco-Egyptian polymath; alchemists often cited him to emphasize that earthly success requires divine favor and cosmic alignment</note> says that no one should claim the knowledge of this art for themselves unless it has been given to them by God. There are also many who, following the literal word of the Philosophers, treat and work upon diverse materials; nonetheless they err, and will continue to err, because they do not understand the vocabulary of the Philosophers, nor can they uncover their true intention.

Many, however, have spoken of common <term>strong waters</term> <note>aqua fortis; typically refers to nitric acid or other corrosive mineral acids</note>, believing the whole secret to consist in them, but they have fallen into the greatest error: for no other strong water enters our <term>magistery</term> <note>the master-process of the Great Work</note> except our **Philosophical water**, which is called the **water of life**, and our **sharpest vinegar** <note>original: "acetum acerrimum"; a highly purified or "philosophical" solvent, not common table vinegar</note>, without which nothing will be perfected in the art.

Nevertheless, many are skilled at extracting strong waters; some indeed extract them from **vitriol and nitre** <note>the standard ingredients for making nitric acid</note>, and others from **cinnabar** <note>mercury sulfide</note>. But this is ultimately worthless, because these waters are highly corrosive on account of the impurity of the matter from which they are made. They can never be called "water of life," because they are more useful for destroying metals than for supplying them with life. For this reason, those who use them for the transmutation of metals err in two ways: first, because the materials from which these waters were made or extracted are not yet separated from all impurities; and that which is impure can in no way give life. This is because every impure thing is a poison—indeed, they contain a great poison for the **matter** <meta>catchword: riæ (matter)</meta>

<column-break/>

-> 429 <-

of this nature. But that which gives life to metals is, without doubt, something most pure which must contain life within itself; for this reason, it communicates and supplies life to the metals. Our **water of life**, or our **sharpest vinegar**, is not, nor can it be, of the nature of common strong waters.

**Raymond** <note>likely referring to Raymond Lully (c. 1232–1315), a major figure to whom many alchemical treatises were attributed</note> indeed says that his water is composed and extracted from a certain mass containing the **four Elements**: and this water is only found by those who are expert in the art. This water is called **lunar water** <note>original: "aqua lunaria"</note> because of its clarity and brilliance; it is also named the **water of life** because it is always "living," and by its vitality, it gives life to all metals. Even dead metals rise again from it once they have been added to it.

This water is also called "vegetable" <note>referring to the "Vegetable Stone" or the life-force inherent in the solvent</note> by many: by which the second Element is separated from the mass and then joined to it. And truly I tell you that this water is the strongest of all, and it is the solvent for all metals. Afterwards, it is congealed together with them, and they become but one single nature. But you must join them according to the appetite of **nature**, and not according to your own personal intention; otherwise, the conjunction will cause you harm.

Then, you must contemplate what sort of matter it is from which this **holy water** <note>original: "aqua benedicta"; here referring to a purified alchemical solvent rather than a religious one</note> is extracted, and always consider mineral and metallic things, and without a doubt you will find this matter.

Having obtained the matter, extract its **spirit** according to the art; afterward, the **phlegm** <note>a watery, tasteless distillate</note>, and finally, our **oil** or **sharpest vinegar**, and thus you will have three elements; for the fourth element remains at the bottom, which is called the <term>dead head</term> <note>original: "caput mortuum"; the useless metallic or earthy residue left after distillation</note>. This spirit, however, is called our **vegetable water**, as well as our **lunar water**, and **water of life**. This water, which is named the **burning spirit** by some Philosophers, should be reserved for the **white** <note>the *albedo* or white stage of the Great Work, associated with silver</note>; and our sharpest vinegar for the **red** <note>the *rubedo* or final red stage, associated with gold</note>.

Although it is always silver, it is not the *original* silver, because through corruption a change occurs from imperfection to perfection.

Toward perfection, and from perfection toward a most perfect nature, silver tends; and from a perfect quality, through the medium of putrefaction, it is led to a most perfect quality: Afterward it passes into a **medicine**, and from that medicine—or essence—other imperfect metals are perfected; and this is to change from an imperfect state into a perfect state, and to ascend from the perfect to the most perfect. The Philosophers have said: make the **volatile** <note>original: "volatili"; substances that vaporize or escape when heated</note> **fixed** <note>original: "fixum"; substances that remain stable and solid under high heat</note>, and make the fixed volatile. *Here is the second Letter of the said Most Reverend Archpriest, Master Antonius de Abatia, written to the seekers of the Chemical Art: On the method of making gold.*

Since, my dearest ones, in the preceding Letter I told you many reasons of this art: yet now I still say to you that without the help of God nothing can be found, as **Raymond Lully** <note>Raimundus Lullius (c. 1232–1315) was a major philosopher and polymath to whom many influential alchemical treatises were later attributed</note> says.

Now, by my Catholic faith, even if my whole body were a tongue, I could never tell how many there are laboring in improper matter—it is as if they wanted a human to be generated from a horse! And yet, many do labor with the proper matter, but they make an addition of some other thing to this matter, joining it with foreign substances, and thus they lose the work entirely. However, we must leave such people in their error, because they will never work correctly. of this art must always flee the **sophisticated way** <note>the path of false or deceptive alchemy</note>, but must fix his whole care on the direct way. For this reason, our art is reserved in the hands of God; for God gives this science according to His own judgment, and He takes it away from the proud and from those who are empty of all justice and goodness. matter: it is called the <term>first volatile water</term> <note>original: "prima aqua volatilis"; in alchemy, "volatile" refers to a substance that easily vaporizes or escapes when heated</note>, while the other is called the "fixed" part, which is also named "earth" and is called the "ferment." <meta>This page continues the "Second Letter" of Antonius de Abatia, specifically expanding on the chemical marriage of "fixed" and "volatile" substances. # 454
## Anthony of Abatia

In the fixed part, however, a natural fire is hidden which dries out the moist part and separates it from all superfluous humidity. The same occurs in the volatile part in which the natural humidity resides, which separates the thicker, terrestrial, and superfluous substance from the fixed part of the matter of the stone. Then, once the superfluous materials have been separated, the pure substance of the one is joined to the pure substance of the other, and they become one whole and integrated compound. By means of the proper operation, this compound becomes **fixed** <term>fixed: in alchemy, a substance that has been rendered non-volatile, meaning it no longer evaporates or changes when exposed to fire</term>, which is what we call "our stone." 

Nevertheless, it must not be entirely fixed; otherwise, it would have no way to enter into another matter and could not grant it perfection. For where the "entry" of the stone is missing, perfection is also lacking—a fact very well known to the wise masters of this art. From these discourses, it can be gathered that metal is generated from a moist matter and a dry matter which, when joined together and **digested** <term>digested: a process of slow, constant heating intended to mature or "ripen" a substance, mimicking natural geothermal processes</term> by nature, generate a material that is fusible—either fixed or not yet fixed—and this occurs according to the degree of nature’s fire. But when nature's fire has been strong, it then generates a fixed matter because the superfluous volatile parts are separated by it; thus, a perfect metal is made, whether **red** or **white** <note>original: "rubrum sive album"; these colors refer to the two highest grades of alchemical transformation: the "white work" resulting in silver and the "red work" resulting in gold</note>.

<column-break/>

# 455
## Second Letter

So it is in the operation of our stone. But how can this union of two contrary materials be achieved? To tell the truth, this happens in two ways that have already been mentioned before and very clearly demonstrated: namely, through their conjunction and their digestion with a gentle fire. In this way, the moist becomes dry, and the dry becomes moist, and they are united and fixed together.

For this reason, **Aristotle** <note>original: "Aristoteles in quarto de metheor."; referring to Book IV of *Meteorology*, a text that was central to medieval alchemy for its theories on how heat and cold act on the elements</note> says in the fourth book of *Meteorology* that digestion is the proper perfection of natural heat, in which nature has joined the dry with the moist—qualities in which cold and heat are also present. Therefore, it happens thus in our materials, even though they seem contrary. 

Know then, dearest brothers, that contraries are never joined except through a **medium** <note>medium: a middle or bridging substance that shares characteristics of both extremes, allowing them to bond</note>, and the medium between the dry and the moist is the "hot and moist," which is called **radical moisture** <term>radical moisture: *humidum radicale*; the fundamental life-force or essential fluid thought to exist in all living things and metals, necessary for growth and stability</term>, which nature has enclosed in all things. Therefore, where this radical moisture is, nature is also there; and where nature is, radical moisture is also there.

These words, however, are not—and cannot be—understood by the ignorant. For this reason, it is said that one ought not to **cast pearls** <note>original: "margaritas projicere ad [pedes]"; a reference to the biblical warning in Matthew 7:6 against "casting pearls before swine," common in alchemical texts to justify keeping secrets from the uninitiated</note> before...

<summary>Antonius explains that the Philosopher's Stone is created by balancing fixed (earthy) and volatile (moist) substances through natural fire and "digestion." He cites Aristotle to argue that a "radical moisture" acts as the necessary bridge to unite these opposing elements.</summary>

--- Page 238 ---
<meta>This page continues the alchemical discourse of Antonio de Abatia, explaining how the process of putrefaction leads to a "regeneration" or renewal of the substance's form. It bridges the philosophical concept of "privation" to the practical application of the alchemical Art.</meta>

# Antonio de Abatia

elevating subtle matters and **calcining** <term>calcining: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in the presence of air to reduce it to a powder or "ash"</term> thick ones; once the separation and purification are completed, the whole **composite** <term>composite: the mixture of chemical substances within the alchemical vessel</term> is stripped of its first form, and this is the **regeneration** of this composite and the renewal of its form. However, many claim that a grain of wheat is generated without a grain of wheat, and they err greatly, because that is a work of nature and not of **Art** <term>Art: the practice of alchemy, viewed as a human skill that mimics and accelerates natural processes</term>. But since nature has shown us her matter already procreated by her, we ought to take this matter, so that through Art we can multiply its power, and we may work according to the nature or kind of the matter. And because the intention of nature is to bring its composite to full perfection, this cannot happen in the mineral kingdom except over many years; but with Art mediating, the time can be shortened. And thus, through Art, we can do in the mineral kingdom in a few days what nature cannot do through the span of a thousand years or more.

By these words indeed, (Dearest brothers), you can easily understand the reason why I could not produce gold at the beginning of my work, and why I made white gold rather than yellow, as I already declared to you in my first letter.

<column-break/>

# Second Letter

I was involved in an error because I did not recognize the powers of the **volatile** <term>volatile: substances that easily vaporize or "fly away" when heated</term> materials, which I ought to have separated entirely from the **fixed** <term>fixed: substances that resist the fire and do not vaporize</term> matter that was to be calcined, and afterward the water was to be joined with the **luminaries** <note>In alchemy, the "Luminaries" usually refer to the Sun (Gold) and the Moon (Silver)</note>; that is, species with its own species; but instead, I mixed the water of one with the water of the other. And this I tell you, so that you do not fall into the same error. After several days, I thought within my mind, after many prayers, that I ought to join this volatile water with the luminary of its own species and not otherwise: Then I recalled to memory that I had read in the books of the Philosophers that genus must be mixed with genus, species with species, and color with similar color. Then, by reading the **Letter of Archelaus** <note>Archelaus was a legendary figure in alchemical literature, often cited for his instructions on the "composition" of the stone</note>, I recognized that my operation was not according to the intention of the Philosophers. Afterward, I corrected my error by studying the books of the Philosophers diligently, and I prayed to God that He might wish to direct me onto the true path, which happened to me by His grace and charity: to Him be eternal glory. These, therefore, are the words of this philosopher Archelaus: "My son, you will find something of great power and utility in the beginning of the process of the work, if [you pour] fresh water upon..."

<summary>Antonio explains that alchemy ("Art") accelerates nature's slow mineral processes and confesses his early mistake of mixing incompatible volatile and fixed substances, a realization he reached through prayer and the study of Archelaus.</summary>

### Here are certain Annotations on the two Letters of the Most Reverend Master Antonio de Abatia.

This author indeed wrote two letters; in the first, he demonstrates that he could not make **gold**, but he made **silver** which he calls <gloss>white gold <note>original: "aurum album"</note></gloss>. Afterward, in the second Letter, he says he has made gold, and that because of the difficulty of the art, he was unable to make gold the first time.

In truth, this art is difficult, though it is not laborious; and this difficulty arises from the materials not being known; and later, once they are known, making the artificial composition so that the **Composite of the Philosophers** <note>original: "compositum Philosophorum"; refers to the final alchemical mixture or the Stone itself</note> might be created.

Nevertheless, those who wish to set sail upon the sea of this art and arrive at the desired port must know the true paths so they do not fall into danger, and they must wait for the suitable time for sailing. But he who is a **Philosopher**, and who judges rightly and knows

...he knows the way through which he will be able to arrive at the desired port; he always avoids danger and follows a calm path. He ought not to be ignorant of the regions in which the **Philosophers** <note>Alchemists often referred to themselves as "Philosophers" to distinguish their spiritual and natural science from mere "puffers" or gold-seekers.</note> wish to rest, nor of the natures of the waters of this sea; nor should he flee from the **echeneis fish** <note>original: "piscem echeneidem"; also known as the remora or suckerfish. But so that he may accomplish this, he must use a hook: that is, he must have a great provision of suitable instruments. Furthermore, the Philosopher rightly recognizes that our materials consist of **two substances in one subject**, united by nature, which substances must be purified before we join them together. One of these is called the **volatile**, while the other is named the **fixed**. The first is **water**, the other indeed is **earth**, and they are of one nature. 

For this reason, the Author said in his first Letter that he had worked upon the water with its own humidity, and thus he erred in the making of **gold**; but he never would have been able to extract the perfect **juice of lunaria** <term>original: "succum lunariæ"; literally "moon-plant juice," a symbolic term for the mercurial essence or "white" stage of the work</term> without this material which is called **Black blacker than black** <note>original: "Nigrum nigrius nigro"; this refers to the *nigredo* or putrefaction stage, the required first step of the Great Work where the matter decomposes and turns pitch black.</note>. ...only that from that blackest matter the **juice of lunaria** <term>original: "succus lunariæ"; literally "juice of the moon-plant," a symbolic term for a mercurial essence used in the "white" or silver stage of the work</term> is extracted, along with the **rectified water of life** <term>original: "aqua vitæ rectificatæ"; usually referring to distilled alcohol, but here used for a highly purified alchemical solvent</term>; first the **phlegm** <note>In early chemistry, 'phlegm' referred to the tasteless, watery distillate that comes off first during heating.</note> is extracted, then the **vinegar** which remains with the dregs; by certain **Philosophers** <note>Alchemists often called themselves "Philosophers" to signal their pursuit of natural and divine wisdom.</note>, this vinegar is called **fresh honey**, **miraculous oil**, and the **sulfur of nature**.

   Nevertheless, the craftsman should note that from the dissolution of silver or gold in the **juice of lunaria**, a great utility is brought forth, and this juice is called **our aqua fortis** <note>original: "aqua fortis nostra"; "strong water." While this often meant nitric acid, in this context it refers to a specialized alchemical solvent "fortified" by the artist.</note>: but why does a great utility come from this dissolution? The first reason is because this water of ours is impregnated by the **spirit of the quintessence** of gold or silver, which spirits have entrance into our water so that it may be under the form of the body of gold or silver: and when it has been separated from its body through distillation, the spirits remain in the water, which dissolves bodies more promptly than before. Here, however, a **beautiful secret** lies hidden: for if anyone can have some quantity of this water, it will suffice forever, because the more this water is worked, the more it is perfected, and the more it is perfected, the
<meta>catchword: magis (more)</meta>

---

<page-num>477</page-num>
<header>Antonius de Abatia. 477</header>

**more** it dissolves: and he who once possesses this will no longer be in need.

   The second reason is that when the water has been joined to the bodies of gold or silver, and afterwards separated from them, it acquires a greater **subtlety** with the preservation of its spirits, which are never lost even when joined to bodies later.

   Here also another **secret** <term>original: "arcanum"; a deep mystery or specialized medicinal/alchemical secret</term> lies hidden: namely, so that the power of this water is not diminished, and its spirit is not lost, it ought to be enclosed in a well-sealed vessel with the **calx of gold** <note>A "calx" is the fine powder or oxide left after a metal has been roasted or "calcined" at high heat.</note>, or with the calx of silver.

   Thirdly, because gold and silver are multiplied and increased in weight, and from this increase the craftsman can be sufficiently sustained until he reaches the completion of his work. Therefore the **Philosopher** says that the water ought to be impregnated by the **soul of the body**, so that you may be able to live until the **stone** <term>original: "lapis"; the Philosopher's Stone, the legendary ultimate goal of the alchemical Great Work</term> is finished; nevertheless, if it is joined with its own similar nature, and recently composed, from it a **divine thing** is made, such that no one could even imagine.

Then separate the juice of <term>moonwort (lunaria)<note>original: lunariæ. A plant traditionally associated with the moon and silver, but frequently used in alchemical recipes for its supposed transformative properties.</note></term> from the <term>phlegm<note>original: phlegmate. In early chemistry, "phlegm" refers to the tasteless, watery distillate produced during the heating of substances, often considered an impurity to be removed.</note></term> by distillation in a water bath, with gentle heat, until no more phlegm is distilled; this is the sign of separation. This phlegm is most perfect, possessing the power of dissolving, and with it gold or silver can easily be dissolved.

Afterward, take one part of this solution with 100 parts of purified <term>mercury (quicksilver)</term>, and in a long-necked vessel over an ash fire, the entire mercury will be <term>fixed<note>original: fixabitur. Likewise, join and mix one part of the said dissolved gold with 6 parts of <term>sublimate<note>original: sublimati. Repeat this until the whole remains fixed at the bottom. This will be a <term>medicine (tincture)<note>original: medicina. In alchemy, a "medicine" is not for healing the body, but a concentrated substance (a powder or elixir) used to "heal" or transform base metals into gold.</note></term>, one part of which is cast upon 100 parts of mercury, and it will become the finest gold.

### Another Secret.

Dissolve one ounce of the purest <term>gold<note>original: folis (of the sun).</note></term> in our **philosophical aqua fortis** <note>original: aqua forti... Philofophica. ### *Another description by another Author.*

Moonwort <note>original: "Lunaria"</note> grows in the form depicted here, at the height of one palm, having six leaves on each side, and three flowers; and the leaves are round and notched <note>original: "denticulata"; having a serrated or tooth-like edge</note>, and its root is one finger long and of the same thickness. One part of the leaf is green, but the other is red. It has many properties, but it should especially be noted that in any place on earth where some treasure has been hidden, and moonwort is carried there—whether unexpectedly or by design—the earth will be moved just as moles move it; indeed, in that very place is the treasure.

Furthermore, it opens all locks without difficulty.

### *Admonition.*

On the Day of Saint John <note>Midsummer, June 24th.</note>, according to the old style <note>The Julian calendar, used before the Gregorian reform.</note>, at midnight, mines <note>original: "fodinæ"</note> of gold, or silver, or other metals are recognized thus: namely, in those places certain lamps seem to sparkle, and other lamps shine like burning coals, and

<column-break/>

<page-num>489</page-num>
<header>Secrets.</header>
<meta>Catchword: Gold</meta>

the richer mines are brighter and deeper.

### *A secret for obtaining the fern with its seed.*

On the eve of Saint John, of the old style, take both ferns <note>Likely referring to the male and female fern (Dryopteris and Athyrium), which were thought to produce "invisible" seeds.</note> with their soil, and let them be brought home at night, and placed upon a table covered with a linen cloth; and without doubt its seed is produced, which is found upon the cloth.

### *Concerning the knowledge of the conjunction of the Lights.*

A rod of vine-wood <note>original: "virga ligni sarmenti"</note> is to be held in the hand around the <term>conjunction of the lights<note>original: "conjunctionis Luminarium." In astrology/alchemy, the "lights" are the Sun and the Moon; their conjunction refers to the New Moon.</note></term>, as is taught in the Almanac; and at the moment in which the conjunction occurs, the rod will break, and the bark will be removed, at which time the seed ought to be sown, and the things to be joined must then be joined. And this also happens in the first, second, and last part of the moon, as well as in its fullness.

Then <term>putrefy<note>To break down or rot a substance as the first step of the alchemical process.</note></term>, divide, cleanse, and join.

## Potable Gold.

Geber <note>A Latinized name for Jabir ibn Hayyan, the "Father of Chemistry," whose writings were the foundation of medieval alchemy.</note> says that this <note>Potable or drinkable gold, a legendary medicine believed to grant longevity.</note> can be made with coals that have been quenched in salt water, and by extracting the "spirit of salt" <note>original: "spiritum salis"; likely hydrochloric acid</note> from them; and this spirit will dissolve gold, which is most excellent for curing all human diseases and does not harm the human body. Others indeed take the powder of calcined <note>heated to a high temperature to reduce to powder</note> bricks and quench it in salt water, and extract the spirit of salt for the same effect. However, this operation requires purification, washing, and sweetening <note>original: "edulcorationem"; the process of washing out acids or salts from a precipitate</note> with sweet things.
